JalRakshak: Project Handbook (v2.0)

Intelligent Water Resource Allocation and Scheduling: the whole project, from basics to viva level, including everything v2.0 added for a water department.
Team HydroLab · B.Tech CSE · PBL, Semester 5 · Subjects: Operating Systems and DBMS

What this document is. A complete teaching guide to your code at version 2.0 (git commit 9b05e7a, about 12,500 lines without tests). It replaces the v1.0 handbook. Every statement comes from reading the actual files: scheduler/ (C++), backend/ (Python/FastAPI), db/ (SQL), frontend/ (React), ml/, proxy/, backup/ and scripts/. Nothing is invented. Anything not verified is labelled that way.

Test evidence used in this handbook was produced on 18 October 2026 by running the real test suites on the v2.0 code in a Linux test environment:

  • C++ scheduler tests: 10,425 checks in 33 groups, 0 failures.
  • Backend tests: 77 passed, against a real PostgreSQL 16 (20 of them new in v2.0).
  • ML tests: 11 passed.
  • Concurrency demo: re-run. With locks, 2 parallel commits produce 1 run and 80,000 L handed out; with locks removed, 2 runs and 160,000 L (double allocation).
  • Browser walkthrough of every new v2.0 screen (15 October 2026): all steps passed, no Content-Security-Policy violations, no page errors, no sideways scrolling on a 390 px phone.

The project has not yet been run on your Windows laptop with Docker. The HTTPS profile, the backup container and GitHub CI have also not been run. These are marked "not verified" where it matters.

How to read the labels

LabelMeaning
CodeConfirmed by reading the source code.
ConfigInferred from configuration files: Dockerfiles, docker-compose.yml, Caddyfile, nginx template, CI workflow, environment variables.
Docs onlyStated in documentation, but not backed by code.
UncertainNot verified, or information is missing.
ExplicitOS concept that our code implements itself.
IndirectOur code uses an OS/DBMS mechanism (we call it; the OS or DBMS does the work).
TheoreticalRelevant to explain the design, but nothing in our code touches it.
Not implementedNot in the project.
PartialImplemented in a limited form.
FutureCould be added later.
New in v2.0Added by version 2.0 (governance, supply timetable, field data, security and privacy).

The purple boxes headed "Simple bhasha mein" explain a hard point in Hinglish. Green "Viva tip" boxes tell you what an examiner is likely to ask. Every phase ends with a summary, the concepts to remember, and five check questions with answers. Try answering before you open each answer.

Preliminary inspection

1. What the project is

JalRakshak ("protector of water") decides how a city's limited water is shared. It works at two levels: Code

  1. Organisation level (since v0.1). Hospitals, schools, housing colonies, shops, factories and parks request water from a reservoir. Each request is treated like a process in an operating system, and the reservoir's supply pipeline like the CPU they compete for. Four scheduling rules (FCFS, Priority, Round Robin, Water-aware) are compared and an administrator applies one.
  2. Zone level (new in v2.0). A daily supply timetable decides which zone of the city gets piped water during which hours, within each source's daily release, its pump capacity and each zone's inlet main. Zones that get too little are sent tankers.

Around these two decisions, v2.0 adds what a water department asks for before a pilot: an approved water policy (maker-checker), officer overrides with reasons, printable decision records, sensor and meter data, a zone map, two-factor sign-in, HTTPS, a least-privilege database user, backups, DPDP privacy rights, an incident register and a Hindi interface for organisations. New in v2.0

4. Application architecture

  Browser: React app (nginx, port 3000, strict CSP)          Field gateway / SCADA (scada_simulator.py)
      |  HTTPS via Caddy (optional "https" profile)              |  POST /telemetry/readings
      |  HTTP + JSON, "Authorization: Bearer <token>"            |  header X-Device-Key
      v                                                          v
  FastAPI backend (Uvicorn, port 8000) -- rate limiter, security headers, admin 2FA guard
      |        \----- child process + pipes -----> C++ scheduler binary
      |                                            modes: plan (fcfs, priority, round_robin,
      |                                            water_aware, manual) | timetable
      |  SQL through psycopg2 as the restricted login "jal_app" (owner login only for upgrades)
      v
  PostgreSQL 16 (24 tables, triggers, partial unique indexes)
      ^                         ^
      |                         |  pg_dump every 24 h -> backups volume (14 days)
  ML pipeline (batch job)   backup container

It is still a 3-tier web application:

  • presentation (React, served by nginx);
  • logic (FastAPI + the C++ scheduler);
  • data (PostgreSQL).

v2.0 adds a second kind of client (field devices that push readings), a reverse proxy for HTTPS, and a backup process. Code Config

ConceptClassificationEvidence

MultithreadingIndirect (FastAPI thread pool); explicit in teststest_postgres.py
Deadlock prevention by lock orderingPartialreservoir row is always locked before request rows; the same order in telemetry
Time as an input to security (time-based one-time passwords, monotonic clock for rate limits)Explicit New in v2.0mfa.py, security.py
Background (daemon-like) process with a sleep loopConfig New in v2.0backup/backup.sh
SJF, preemptive priority, multilevel queuesNot implementednone
Paging, virtual memory, page tablesTheoretical (the OS does it underneath)none
Process isolationIndirect (Docker containers)docker-compose.yml

All of the following were read in full for this handbook:

  • v1 core: service.py (commit_allocation), sequential.cpp, water_aware.cpp, round_robin.cpp, scheduler.cpp, scheduler_client.py, auth.py, portal.py, db.py, migrations.py, main.py

8. Missing information and uncertainties

  • Team members, guide and university report format. Not in the folder. Uncertain
  • Real-world data. Still none. The demo consumption history is generated (synthetic). v2.0 can accept real meter data (sensors, CSV import) and uses it once a zone has 120 days, but no real data has been loaded. Zone sizes, pump capacities and map shapes in the demo are illustrative. Code
  • The water policy values are demo values. Policy v1 reproduces v1.0 behaviour. The 135 L/person/day norm is the CPHEEO urban norm (as written in the policy note); the priorities and shares are not an official order. Code
  • Running on your laptop. v2.0 has not been confirmed with Docker on Windows. Uncertain
  • Not run in the test environment: the Caddy HTTPS profile, the backup container, the restricted login jal_app through the real psycopg2 driver (the tests use a psql-based stand-in), and GitHub CI. Uncertain
  • Things only the department can do (listed in docs/compliance.md): a CERT-In-empanelled security audit, NIC / MeitY-empanelled hosting, Parichay single sign-on, encryption of 2FA secrets with an outside key, a formal GIGW check, legal review of the privacy notice, connection to real SCADA. Not implemented
  • Literature research on how Indian water utilities really allocate water was not done in depth. Statements about practice are marked as assumptions. Uncertain

QuestionAnswer
1. What is it?

A web application for a city water department where:

  • organisations request water from a reservoir;
  • the department compares four allocation rules on the same requests and applies one, or changes the plan with a recorded reason;
  • a daily zone supply timetable says which zone gets piped water at which hours, and tankers are planned for zones that get too little New in v2.0;
  • the rules (priorities, guaranteed shares, the per-person norm) come from an approved water policy New in v2.0;
  • the system stores every decision safely, forecasts demand, flags possible leaks, and accepts sensor and meter readings.
2. Real-world problemWater scarcity at the distribution level. When demand is higher than supply (example: 80,000 L asked, 50,000 L available; or a city of 135,000 people needing 18.2 million litres a day when 12 million are released), someone must decide who gets how much, when, and in which order, and be able to justify it later.
3. Who faces it
  • Water department operators and engineers, who must decide.
  • Senior officers, who approve policy and answer audits and RTI questions.
  • Organisations that depend on supply: hospitals, schools, housing colonies, shops, factories, parks.
  • Residents of each zone, who need to know their supply hours.
4. How it's handled todayAssumption, not researched in depth Fixed zone schedules, habit, or roughly first come first served, often on paper or spreadsheets, with no recorded reason for each decision. Many Indian cities have intermittent supply (water for a few hours a day per zone), so a zone timetable is the normal unit of planning.
5. Limitations of that
  • FCFS ignores importance (in our sample a factory takes 20,000 L first).
  • Pure priority starves low-priority users.
  • Nobody can compare "what would another rule have done?"
  • Two operators can double-allocate.
  • Priorities are decided informally, not from an approved order.
  • No audit trail, no forecasting, no link to meter data.
6. How we address them
  • Four rules run on identical data and are shown side by side before anything is saved.
  • Water-aware rule with a starvation guard; the guaranteed share now comes from the policy class.
  • Policy changes need a second officer to approve (maker-checker).
  • An officer can override a plan, but must give a reason; it goes into a printable decision record.
  • Zone timetable within source, pump and pipe limits; tanker orders for short zones.
  • Locked database transactions; an append-only audit log.
  • Demand forecast, leak alerts, sensor-offline and complaint-cluster alerts.
  • A panel for each organisation (English or Hindi) showing requests and its zone's supply hours.
7. Objectives

(1) Implement OS scheduling rules plus a new water-aware rule on one shared engine.

(2) Measure them honestly: waiting time, fairness, importance-weighted delivery, starvation, missed deadlines.

(3) Make concurrent commits safe.

(4) Forecast demand and detect leaks.

(5) Provide secure, role-based panels.

(6) v2.0 Make the system acceptable to a water authority: policy-driven and accountable decisions, zone-wise supply planning, real data inputs, and security and privacy fit for a government system.

8. Users
  • Requesters (role requester): staff of one organisation.
  • Administrators (role admin): water department officers. v2.0 needs two of them for a policy change (one proposes, another approves). The demo has a second officer, approver@jalrakshak.local.
  • Field devices (not people): level sensors and flow meters that send readings with their own key.
9. Modules
  • Scheduler (C++): allocation rules, manual plans, zone timetable.
  • Allocation service, policy, supply network and tankers, telemetry.
  • Auth with two-factor sign-in; privacy; security (rate limits, incidents, operations).
  • User panel and admin panel (11 tabs).
  • ML pipeline; database; experiments.
  • Infrastructure: nginx with CSP, Caddy for HTTPS, backup container.
10. Why usefulMakes a hard trade-off visible and measurable, makes the decision safe and accountable (who decided, under which policy, why, and what the alternatives were), and turns a reservoir release into a published zone timetable that residents can see.
11. Limitations
  • Data is still synthetic in the demo; real meter data can be loaded but none has been.
  • No pipe hydraulics (pressures, valves); limits are per source and per zone inlet.
  • Soft deadlines; hand-chosen Water-aware weights (now editable through policy).
  • Water-aware is not best on every measure.
  • No email reset, no connection pool, no government SSO, no formal security audit.
12. Scope

In scope:

  • allocation decisions per reservoir, with comparison of rules and overrides;
  • zone timetables across several sources, and tanker orders;
  • policy with approval; decision records; pilot (shadow) mode and indicators;
  • sensor/meter ingestion, CSV import, zone map;
  • safe storage, security and privacy functions; two panels.

Out of scope:

  • controlling physical pumps and valves (the system plans; people operate);
  • billing;
  • hydraulic modelling of the pipe network;
  • a real SCADA connection (a simulator stands in).

The core analogy (memorise this table)

Operating systemJalRakshakWhere in code
ProcessA water requeststruct Request in model.hpp
CPUThe single supply pipelinerun_sequential() serves one request at a time
Burst timeLitres ÷ flow rate (500 L/min)finish = start + grant / flow_rate_lpm
Arrival timeWhen the request was madearrival_time (minutes)
PriorityClass of organisation, from the approved policy (hospital 5 … park 1)users.priority, set by policy.apply_class_priorities()
Time quantum2,000 L per turn in Round Robinquantum_litres
Ready queuePending requests that have arrivedcollect_ready()
StarvationA request that gets 0 Lunserved_count
Aging (to stop starvation)Fairness factor + guaranteed share per classwater_aware.cpp
Time-slot reservation of a shared device v2.0Hours of pump capacity given to each zone in the timetabletimetable.cpp, step 2

One big difference from CPU scheduling: water is consumed. A CPU gives time and is still there afterwards; litres given away are gone. That's why our schedulers also decide how much each request gets (full, partial or nothing), not only the order. The timetable makes the same split explicit: step 1 decides how much each zone gets, step 2 decides when.

A. 30-second explanation

"JalRakshak helps a water department share limited water when demand is higher than supply.

  • We treated it like CPU scheduling: each request is a process, the pipeline is the CPU. Four schedulers in C++, including our own Water-aware rule that never leaves anyone with zero water.
  • Version 2 adds a zone-wise daily supply timetable with tankers, an approved water policy with maker-checker, officer overrides with reasons, sensor data, and government-grade security: two-factor sign-in, HTTPS, a least-privilege database user, backups and DPDP privacy rights.
  • PostgreSQL stores every decision, and its row locks make sure two operators can never hand out the same water twice."

B. 2-minute explanation

"When a reservoir has 50,000 litres but users ask for 80,000, someone must decide who gets what. Usually it's first come, first served, which can let a factory take water while a hospital waits.

We modelled this as an OS scheduling problem. Each request is like a process with an arrival time, a priority, an urgency and a deadline; the supply pipeline is like a CPU delivering 500 litres a minute. Our C++ scheduler implements first come first served, non-preemptive priority, round robin with a 2,000-litre quantum, and our own Water-aware rule, which scores requests on five factors and keeps a guaranteed share in reserve for everyone still waiting.

The FastAPI backend runs the scheduler as a child process through pipes and saves the chosen plan in one locked transaction. We proved the locks work: with locks 80,000 litres were allocated; without them, 160,000.

For version 2 we reviewed the project as a water authority would. Priorities and guaranteed shares now come from a versioned water policy that one officer proposes and a different officer approves. An officer can change a plan but must give a reason, and the system produces a decision record listing the policy, the reason and the alternatives that were compared. A second scheduler mode builds a daily zone timetable: with 12 million litres for 135,000 people, every zone gets about 89 litres per person in one continuous block of hours. If a zone falls below the tanker trigger, the system orders tanker loads. Sensors can push reservoir levels and meter readings with their own keys.

Security and privacy were raised too: two-factor sign-in, rate limits, HTTPS through Caddy, a database login that cannot touch the audit log, daily backups, consent and data export under the DPDP Act, and a Hindi interface. Our honest limits: the demo data is synthetic, and the department would still need its own security audit, hosting and real data."

C. Detailed technical explanation (viva examiner)

  1. Data model.
    • water_requests belong to users (organisations), which belong to zones. Zones are fed by a reservoirs source (v2.0).
    • A committed plan is one scheduler_runs row (with its policy, override reason and comparison of all rules) plus one allocations row per request.
    • v2.0 adds 8 tables: policies, supply_timetables, tanker_trips, devices, readings, login_challenges, privacy_requests, security_incidents (24 tables in total).
    • Integrity is enforced by the schema, e.g. CHECK (available_litres >= 0), and by two partial unique indexes: only one approved policy, only one published timetable per day.
  2. Commit path: service.commit_allocation() runs as one transaction:
    • it locks the reservoir row, then the pending requests (FOR UPDATE);
    • it reads the active policy and gives each request its class's guaranteed share (min_share);
    • it runs the C++ binary with subprocess.run() (JSON through stdin/stdout, 10-second timeout);
    • if the officer changed litres, it checks them (reason ≥ 10 characters, 0 ≤ litres ≤ asked, total ≤ available) and re-runs the plan in the scheduler's manual mode;
    • it also runs the other three rules and stores their metrics as comparison;
    • it writes the run, allocations, statuses, the new water level, notifications and audit rows; then COMMIT. Any exception → ROLLBACK.
  3. Scheduler internals. run_sequential() is a discrete-event simulation with a picker function. FCFS, Priority, Water-aware and Manual differ only in the picker; Round Robin has its own queue loop. main.cpp looks at "mode": no mode → plan; "timetable" → the zone timetable code.
  4. Water-aware. Score = 0.30 priority + 0.25 urgency + 0.15 scarcity + 0.15 population + 0.15 fairness (weights now stored in the policy). Cap = max(own_share × asked, water_left − Σ others' share × asked).
  5. Timetable. Demand = population × 135 L (or metered use). Target = min(demand, inlet capacity × supply hours). Each zone first gets its guaranteed share of the target; the rest is shared by weighted water-filling (weight = priority × (1 − share) × target). Then zones are placed, most important first, in the earliest continuous block of hourly slots that the pump can still carry. Invariants (source release, pump per slot, demand) are checked inside the program.
  6. Concurrency proof. tests/concurrency_demo.py: with locks 1 plan and 80,000 L; without them 2 plans and 160,000 L.
  7. Security. PBKDF2-SHA256 (600,000 iterations); hashed session tokens (12 h); lockout after 5 wrong passwords; TOTP two-factor sign-in; rate limits (20/min on sign-in); CSP and other headers; a least-privilege DB login jal_app; audit log protected by a row trigger, a statement trigger and REVOKE.
  8. ML. Robust z-score leak detection; Random Forest forecast, MAE 1,223 L (5.1%) on synthetic data. v2.0: real meter data replaces generated data for a zone once it has ≥ 120 days.

Journey 2: the administrator allocates (and may override)

  1. The admin signs in. The first time, ForcedPasswordChange makes them choose a new password. If two-factor sign-in is on, a second screen asks for the 6-digit code.
  2. Allocate tab → POST /allocate/simulate → all 4 rules run. Nothing is written.
  3. Either Apply this plan on one rule, or open Change the plan before applying: pick a starting rule, edit litres, type the reason, apply. Both go to POST /allocate/commit.
  4. Or record the plan in shadow mode (POST /allocate/shadow): stored for pilot comparison, but no water or request changes.
  5. Records tab → Decision record (HTML to print as PDF, or CSV).

Journey 3: changing the water policy (maker-checker)

  1. Officer A: Policy tab → Propose a change (e.g. hospital guaranteed share 0.6, reference "G.O. No. 12/2026") → Submit for approval. Status pending.
  2. Officer A cannot approve it: the server returns 403 "maker-checker".
  3. Officer B signs in → Approve and activate. In one transaction the old policy becomes superseded, the new one approved, and every organisation without a manual exception gets its class's priority. Rejecting needs a reason.

Journey 4: the daily supply timetable and tankers

  1. Supply tab → choose the date and demand source (policy norm × population, or metered use) → optionally change today's release per source → Compute draft (POST /timetables).
  2. Check hours, litres and litres per person per zone → Publish. This withdraws any earlier published timetable for that date and notifies every organisation in each zone of its hours.
  3. Plan tankers for short zones: one order per zone below the trigger (70 L/person in policy v1), with the number of 10,000 L loads needed. Status goes planned → dispatched (zone notified) → delivered.

Journey 5: sensors and meters

  1. Field data tab → register a device (reservoir level sensor or zone flow meter). Its key is shown once.
  2. The gateway (in the demo scripts/scada_simulator.py) sends POST /telemetry/readings with header X-Device-Key. A level reading becomes the reservoir's water level; flow readings become daily metered consumption.
  3. If a device is silent for 30 minutes, an "offline" alert appears and staff enter values by hand.

Journey 6: privacy and two-factor

  1. Profile → Turn on two-factor sign-in → scan the key in an authenticator app → enter a code to confirm.
  2. Profile → Download my data (JSON) or request correction, erasure or a grievance; admins handle them in Compliance.

Worked example 1: the sample allocation (real output)

The seed data has 8 requests: 80,000 L asked, 50,000 L available. Output of service.simulate() on a freshly seeded v2.0 database under policy v1, run on 18 Oct 2026. These are the same numbers as in v1.0, because policy v1 gives every class the same 30% share.

RuleAvg wait (min)Jain fairnessImportance-weightedLeft with 0 LMissed deadlines
FCFS70.250.500.5441
Priority60.20.570.7430
Round robin29.40.910.7101
Water-aware75.10.740.6800

Per-request result of Water-aware, in the order it served them:

#Organisation (priority)AskedGotScore
1City Hospital (5)10,00010,0000.940
2Shanti Apartments (4)15,00015,0000.819
3Rajpur Colony (4)12,00012,0000.764
4Green Valley School (4)6,0001,9000.734
5Central Mall (2)8,0002,4000.583
6Textile Mill (2)5,0001,5000.499
7Town Park (1)4,0001,2000.472
8Metro Steel Works (2)20,0006,0000.436

Dekho: the school got only 1,900 L. Why? After the first three requests, 13,000 L is left.

  • The others still waiting want 8,000 + 5,000 + 4,000 + 20,000 = 37,000 L.
  • Each of them has a 30% guaranteed share (policy v1), so 0.3 × 37,000 = 11,100 L stays in reserve.
  • So the school's cap is 13,000 − 11,100 = 1,900 L.

v2.0 mein agar policy kahe "hospital 0.5, park 0.1", toh har request apne class ka share reserve karegi; formula same hai, bas share alag-alag. Isi wajah se koi bhi zero pe nahi gaya.

Worked example 2: the demo zone timetable (real output)

Demo network: one source (Main Reservoir, usual release 12,000,000 L/day, pump 1,000,000 L/h); North Zone 40,000 people (inlet 600,000 L/h), Central 65,000 (900,000 L/h), South 30,000 (450,000 L/h); supply window 05:00–23:00; norm 135 L/person/day. Output of network.build_draft() on 18 Oct 2026. Code (values are illustrative, not a real city)

12,000,000 L (usual)North5,400,0003,555,55588.9605:00–11:00
Central8,775,0005,777,77788.9711:00–18:00

Metrics: served ratio 0.66 (usual) and 0.33 (drought); Jain fairness between zones 1.00 in both; all 3 zones below the 135 L norm. On the drought day all zones are below the 70 L tanker trigger, so Plan tankers orders 103 loads for North, 167 for Central and 77 for South (10,000 L each), exactly as shown in the browser walkthrough.

Sab zones ko barabar 88.9 L kyun mila? Policy v1 mein har zone ki priority 3 aur guaranteed share 30% hai. Toh weight = 3 × 0.7 × target, yaani target ke proportion mein. Isliye sabko same fraction (66%) mila. Agar kisi zone ki priority badhao, toh usko extra paani pehle milega.

South ka block 17:00 se shuru hai aur Central 18:00 tak chalta hai, yaani 17:00–18:00 mein dono saath. Pump overload toh nahi hua? Calculate karo:

  • Central ko 5,777,777 L chahiye, 900,000 L/h pe. 6 poore ghante = 5,400,000 L, toh last ghante (17–18) mein sirf 377,777 L.
  • Pump 1,000,000 L/h deta hai, toh 17–18 mein 622,223 L capacity bachi.
  • South ka inlet 450,000 L/h leta hai: 622,223 mein fit ho jaata hai. Total = 827,777 L < 1,000,000 L.

Program har slot ke liye yahi check karta hai (free[t]), aur end mein invariant bhi: "pump capacity exceeded" kabhi nahi hona chahiye.

Phase 1 wrap-up

Summary.

  • JalRakshak is a decision-support web app for sharing scarce water, built on an OS scheduling analogy, and in v2.0 extended to zone-wise supply planning and the governance, data and security needs of a water department.
  • The OS part we implemented ourselves is the scheduling simulation (and now slot scheduling of zones), plus the use of child processes, pipes and locks.
  • The DBMS part is substantial: 24 tables, constraints, partial unique indexes, transactions, locks, triggers, DCL.

Remember:

  • request = process; pipeline = CPU; burst = litres ÷ 500;
  • simulate (no save) vs commit (one locked transaction) vs shadow (recorded, no water moves);
  • guaranteed share = starvation guard, now per policy class;
  • timetable: first how much (floors + water-filling), then when (slots);
  • maker-checker: the proposer cannot approve.

Check questions (open each after you answer):

1. What is the burst time of a 6,000 L request?12 minutes, because the pipeline delivers 500 L per minute: 6,000 ÷ 500 = 12. In code: finish = start + grant / flow_rate_lpm in sequential.cpp.
2. Simulate, commit, shadow: which ones change the water level?Only commit. simulate() writes nothing. shadow_plan() writes a run marked committed = false (scenario shadow) for pilot evidence, but doesn't touch the reservoir or request statuses. commit_allocation() changes the water level, statuses, and writes allocations, notifications and audit rows.
3. Who decides an organisation's priority in v2.0?The approved water policy gives each class a priority (hospital 5, school 4, households 4, commercial 2, industry 2, park 1 in policy v1). On approval, apply_class_priorities() copies it to every organisation. An admin can still set an exception in Settings; it is flagged (priority_override) and kept when the policy changes, until reset.
4. Why did every zone get 88.9 L per person on a normal day?12,000,000 L for 18,225,000 L of demand is 66%. All three zones have the same priority (3) and share (30%) in the demo, so the extra water is split in proportion to each zone's target, and every zone ends with the same fraction: 0.66 × 135 ≈ 88.9 L per person.
5. What can an officer NOT do when overriding a plan?Skip the reason (minimum 10 characters), give a request more than it asked or less than 0, or hand out more than the available water in total. _apply_overrides() refuses each of these with a 400 error, and the C++ manual mode checks the total again.

What v2.0 adds: the water-authority requirements

Version 2.0 came from one exercise: we reviewed the v1.0 project as an officer of a water department would before agreeing to a pilot, wrote down what such an officer would ask for, and then implemented it. The full point-by-point map is in docs/compliance.md. This chapter summarises it, with screenshots from the browser walkthrough of 15 Oct 2026. The review itself was written by us, not by a real department.

Three honest labels used below. Implemented + tested means code exists and an automated test proves it. Configured means the files exist (Docker, Caddy, scripts) but we did not run them in the test environment. Department's part means software can't do it: audits, hosting, legal review.

The four requirement areas at a glance

What stays the department's job

  • A CERT-In-empanelled security audit before go-live.
  • Hosting in an NIC / state data centre or a MeitY-empanelled cloud.
  • Parichay / government single sign-on (it would replace our sign-in page; the role checks stay).
  • Encrypting 2FA secrets with a key held outside the database (a code change we can make; key custody is theirs).
  • A formal GIGW / STQC check; legal review of the privacy notice; naming the grievance officer.
  • Connecting the real SCADA (vendor gateway), loading real meter history, and approving the real policy.
  • Maintenance contract, support staff, uptime targets, training.

Viva mein v2.0 ko aise bolo: "Humne apne project ko ek water department ki nazar se dekha. Unke chaar sawaal the: rules kaun banata hai (governance), paani zone-wise kaise jaata hai (timetable), asli data kahan se aayega (sensors), aur system kitna safe hai (security, privacy). Har sawaal ka code aur test hai, aur jo kaam sirf department kar sakta hai, woh humne clearly alag likha hai."

v2.0 chapter wrap-up

Summary. v2.0 answers four areas a water department would raise: governance, distribution, data and security/privacy. Almost everything is implemented and tested; HTTPS and backups are configured but not run here; audit, hosting, SSO and real data remain the department's part.

Remember:

  • the four areas and one feature for each (maker-checker; timetable; device keys; 2FA);
  • "configured" ≠ "verified";
  • the before/after numbers table.
1. Name the four requirement areas of v2.0.Governance (policy, maker-checker, overrides, decision records, pilot), distribution (zone timetable, sources and limits, tankers), data (sensors, meters, CSV, map, complaint signals), security and privacy (2FA, HTTPS, least privilege, backups, DPDP, incidents, Hindi).
2. Which v2.0 features are configured but not verified?The Caddy HTTPS profile and the backup container with its restore scripts (plus the API connecting as jal_app through the real driver).
3. Why does every plan store a policy version?So a decision can always be explained later by the rules in force at that time, even after the policy changes.
4. What can't software alone provide for go-live?An external security audit, government hosting, SSO onboarding, legal review of the privacy notice, real data and an officially approved policy.
5. Which screen shows pilot evidence?The Compliance tab's pilot indicators (plans, override rate, essential demand delivered, requests left empty, complaints and resolution time, minimum L/person, tanker loads, leak alerts), together with shadow-mode runs.

Phase 2 · Complete technology stack analysis

First, the vocabulary: language, framework, library, API, database, server, tool

TermPlain meaningExample from our project
Programming languageA set of rules for writing instructions a computer can run.C++ (scheduler), Python (backend, ML), JavaScript/JSX (frontend), SQL (database)
LibraryReady-made code you call when you need it. You stay in control.pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, psycopg2, React (strictly a UI library)
FrameworkA skeleton that calls your code. You fill in the blanks ("inversion of control").FastAPI: you write def login(...); FastAPI decides when to call it
APIA contract describing how one program can ask another for something.Our HTTP API (95 endpoints such as POST /allocate/commit); also the scheduler's JSON stdin/stdout contract in docs/contracts.md
Database / DBMSA database is organised stored data; a DBMS is the software that manages it safely.PostgreSQL 16 (the DBMS) managing the jalrakshak database
ServerA program that waits for requests and answers them (also used for the machine it runs on).Uvicorn (serves the API on port 8000), nginx (serves the web page on port 3000→80), PostgreSQL server (port 5432), Caddy (optional HTTPS front door on port 443)
Development toolHelps you build, test or ship, but isn't part of the running app.g++, Make, esbuild, Docker, GitHub Actions, PowerShell script

Library ko tum bulate ho; framework tumhe bulata hai.

  • pandas.read_csv() you call yourself.
  • @app.post("/auth/login") sirf register karta hai. Jab browser request bhejta hai tab FastAPI tumhara function call karta hai.

Each technology in detail (12 points each)

Rows: 1 definition · 2 category · 3 why used · 4 problem solved · 5 how it works · 6 where · 7 files/functions · 8 communication · 9 if removed · 10 alternatives · 11 pros/cons · 12 viva point.

C++17

1 DefinitionC++ is a compiled, statically-typed language. "17" is the 2017 version of the standard (gives std::optional, structured bindings, etc.).
2 CategoryProgramming language (systems language).
3 Why hereThe OS-subject part, the schedulers, is written in the language OS courses use. It's fast and deterministic: same input, same output (tested: "all algorithms deterministic").
4 Problem solvedRuns each allocation rule on the request list and returns a plan plus metrics, with strict invariants (never more than available, never more than asked).
5 How it worksg++ translates source to machine code once. The binary then runs directly on the CPU with no interpreter. Memory is handled by STL containers (std::vector, std::deque, std::map) and std::unique_ptr, which free memory automatically (RAII). There is no manual new/delete.
6 Wherescheduler/
7 Files / functions
  • main.cpp: main()
  • scheduler.cpp: make_scheduler(), execute(), check_invariants(), compute_metrics()
  • sequential.cpp: run_sequential()
  • fcfs.cpp, priority.cpp, round_robin.cpp, water_aware.cpp: classes deriving from Scheduler
8 CommunicationReads one JSON document from stdin and writes one to stdout. Exit code 0 means OK; 1 means error JSON.
9 If removedNo allocation plans. The backend raises SchedulerUnavailable ("scheduler binary not found") → HTTP 500.
10 Alternatives
  • Python: simpler, one language less, but slower and less "OS-like".
  • Rust: safer, but the team would need to learn it.
  • Java: needs a JVM.
11 Pros / cons+ speed, control, matches the OS subject, small static binary. − compile step, harder to write, a second language to maintain.
12 Viva point"Each scheduler is a class implementing the abstract Scheduler interface (polymorphism). make_scheduler() is a factory function."

g++ and Make

1 Definitiong++ is the GNU C++ compiler. Make is a tool that runs build commands only for files that changed.
2 CategoryDevelopment / build tools.
3 WhyA standard, free toolchain; the official gcc:13 Docker image includes both.
4 ProblemTurns 8 .cpp files into one executable, plus a test executable.
5 HowMake reads rules ("target: dependencies → command"). Each .cpp compiles to a .o object file, then they are linked into build/jalrakshak-scheduler. Flags: -O2 (optimise) and -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic (strict warnings). -static-libstdc++ embeds the C++ runtime, so the binary runs inside the Python image.
6–7 Wherescheduler/Makefile; stage 1 of backend/Dockerfile (RUN make -C scheduler).
8 CommunicationProduces a file. Docker copies it into the backend image at /usr/local/bin/jalrakshak-scheduler.
9 If removedNo binary, unless compiled by hand.
10 AlternativesCMake (cross-platform projects), clang, MSVC on Windows.
11 Pros / cons+ simple, incremental. − Makefile syntax is old-fashioned; not native on Windows (which is why Docker does the compiling).
12 Viva pointMulti-stage Docker build: compile with the big gcc:13 image, ship only the binary in the slim Python image.

Our own JSON parser (json.hpp)

1 DefinitionA small header-only C++ library we wrote. It represents any JSON value (null, bool, number, string, array, object), parses text and prints text.
2 CategoryLibrary (in-house).
3 WhyZero external dependencies, so the scheduler builds anywhere with just g++.
4 ProblemC++ has no built-in JSON support.
5 HowA recursive-descent parser: it reads one character, decides the value type ({ object, [ array, " string …), and calls itself for nested values.
6–7 Whereinclude/json.hpp (json::Value::parse, dump); model_io.cpp converts JSON ↔ Input/Output structs and validates fields.
8 CommunicationSits between stdin text and the scheduler structs.
9 If removedThe scheduler couldn't read input.
10 Alternativesnlohmann/json (popular, well tested), RapidJSON (faster).
11 Pros / cons+ no dependency, small. − less battle-tested than popular libraries (mitigated by the round-trip test test_json_roundtrip and the fuzz test).
12 Viva pointInput validation happens in model_io.cpp: e.g. non-positive litres, priority outside 1–5 or a duplicate request id cause an error JSON and exit code 1 (test_input_validation).

Python 3.12

1 DefinitionA high-level, interpreted, dynamically-typed language.
2 CategoryProgramming language.
3 WhyThe best ecosystem for both web APIs (FastAPI) and data science (pandas, scikit-learn), so one language serves two parts.
4 ProblemGlue: HTTP, database, the scheduler process, ML.
5 HowCPython compiles source to bytecode and interprets it. The GIL (global interpreter lock) lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, but it is released while waiting on I/O (database, child process). That's why a thread pool still helps a web server.
6–7 Wherebackend/app/*.py, ml/jalml/*.py, experiments/run_experiments.py, all tests.
8 CommunicationHTTP (in), SQL (out), pipes to C++.
9 If removedNothing connects the parts.
10 AlternativesNode.js (JavaScript everywhere, weaker ML), Java/Spring (heavier).
11 Pros / cons+ readable, huge libraries. − slower than C++, the GIL, errors found at run time (mitigated by tests).
12 Viva pointWhy two languages? "C++ for the CPU-bound, OS-style algorithm core; Python for I/O-bound glue and ML."

FastAPI

1 DefinitionA modern Python web framework for building HTTP APIs, based on Starlette (web toolkit) and Pydantic (validation).
2 CategoryWeb framework.
3 WhyLittle code per endpoint; automatic validation, error messages and interactive docs at /docs; dependency injection for database connections and role checks.
4 ProblemTurns HTTP requests into Python function calls and Python results into JSON responses.
5 HowThe router matches method + path to a function. Before calling it, FastAPI resolves each Depends(...): e.g. get_conn opens a DB connection, admin_account checks the token and role. It then validates the JSON body with Pydantic, calls the function, and serialises the return value. Plain def endpoints run in a thread pool, so a slow DB call doesn't block other users.
6–7 Wheremain.py:
  • app = FastAPI(..., lifespan=lifespan)
  • current_account, admin_account, requester_account
  • 11 @app.exception_handlers
  • security_headers middleware
  • CORS middleware
8 CommunicationReceives HTTP from the browser; calls service, auth, portal, admin_service.
9 If removedNo API, so the panels can't work (the C++ and SQL would still work alone).
10 AlternativesFlask (simpler, no built-in validation), Django REST (batteries included, heavier), Express (Node).
11 Pros / cons+ fast to write, typed, auto docs. − sync endpoints share a limited thread pool (about 40 threads by default); async needs care.
12 Viva point"Authorization is a dependency: me=Depends(admin_account). If the role is wrong, FastAPI never calls the endpoint and returns 403."

Uvicorn

1 DefinitionAn ASGI server. ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is the standard way Python async web apps talk to a server.
2 CategoryApplication server.
3 WhyFastAPI needs an ASGI server to listen on a network port.
4 ProblemAccepts TCP connections, parses HTTP, hands requests to FastAPI.
5 HowAn event loop: one thread juggles many connections, waiting on sockets without blocking. FastAPI then moves sync endpoints into worker threads.
6–7 Wherebackend/Dockerfile: CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"].
8 CommunicationSocket :8000 ↔ browser; Python calls ↔ FastAPI.
9 If removedThe app can't receive requests.
10 AlternativesGunicorn with Uvicorn workers (several processes, for production), Hypercorn.
11 Pros / cons+ light, fast. − we run a single process: no multi-core use, no automatic restart.
12 Viva point"Uvicorn is the server; FastAPI is the framework."

Pydantic

1 DefinitionA Python library that validates data against type-annotated classes.
2 CategoryValidation library.
3 WhyRejects bad input before it reaches business logic or the database.
4 ProblemManual if-checks everywhere.
5 HowEach body is a class: requested_litres: float = Field(gt=0, le=10_000_000). Pydantic converts and checks the JSON. On failure FastAPI returns 422 with the field name and reason (shown to users by api.js: describeDetail()).
6–7 Whereschemas.py: MyRequestCreate, LoginBody, ReservoirUpdate, ZoneCreate, AccountCreate, …
8 CommunicationUsed inside FastAPI.
9 If removedBad values would reach SQL; the DB CHECKs would still catch many, but with worse messages.
10 Alternativesmarshmallow, attrs + manual checks.
11 Pros / cons+ declarative, clear errors. − one more layer; rules duplicated in the DB (deliberately: defence in depth).
12 Viva pointThree layers of validation:
  • Pydantic (shape and ranges);
  • service code (business rules, e.g. at most 5 pending requests);
  • PostgreSQL CHECK constraints (last line of defence).

psycopg2

1 DefinitionThe most widely used PostgreSQL driver (adapter) for Python.
2 CategoryDatabase driver / connector.
3 WhyMature, supports %s parameters, transactions, and error codes (pgcode).
4 ProblemPython can't speak PostgreSQL's network protocol by itself.
5 Howpsycopg2.connect(DATABASE_URL) opens a TCP connection and logs in. cursor.execute(sql, params) sends the query with the values passed separately (safely quoted). with conn: means COMMIT on success, ROLLBACK on exception. RealDictCursor returns rows as dicts.
6–7 Wheredb.py:
  • connect(), which retries 5 times, 1 s apart;
  • get_conn(), one connection per HTTP request, always closed;
  • ensure_schema().
Also ml/jalml/pipeline.py: connect().
8 CommunicationPython ↔ PostgreSQL over TCP, at db:5432 inside Docker.
9 If removedNo database access.
10 Alternativespsycopg 3 (newer, async), asyncpg, an ORM (SQLAlchemy) on top.
11 Pros / cons+ explicit SQL; easy to show DBMS concepts. − no connection pool in our code; raw SQL strings.
12 Viva point"We didn't use an ORM on purpose: the SQL is visible, so we can explain every query, lock and transaction."

PostgreSQL 16 (with SQL and PL/pgSQL)

1 DefinitionAn open-source object-relational DBMS. SQL is its query language; PL/pgSQL is its built-in procedural language for functions and triggers.
2 CategoryRDBMS (database server).
3 WhyACID transactions, row-level locks, CHECK constraints, triggers, JSONB, advisory locks. All of these are DBMS-syllabus topics we actually use.
4 ProblemData that must stay correct when many users change it at the same time.
5 How
  • A server process accepts connections and starts one backend process per connection.
  • Data lives in 8 KB pages on disk, cached in shared memory.
  • Changes are first written to the WAL (write-ahead log) for durability.
  • MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) lets readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers.
  • Row locks (FOR UPDATE) make writers wait for each other.
6–7 Wheredb/schema.sql (10 core tables, function load_sample_requests), db/migrate.sql (6 v1.0 tables, trigger, idempotent upgrades), db/seed.sql, db/Dockerfile (scripts in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d).
8 CommunicationTCP 5432 (5433 on your PC); clients: backend, ML job.
9 If removedNothing persists; no locking means double allocation.
10 AlternativesMySQL (similar), SQLite (no real concurrent writers, no row locks), MongoDB (no joins or foreign keys, weaker fit).
11 Pros / cons+ correctness features, free, standard SQL. − a separate server to run; backups and tuning are our job.
12 Viva point"The database itself refuses a negative water level (CHECK (available_litres >= 0)), even if the application had a bug. Tested: test_database_itself_refuses_a_negative_water_level."

pandas and NumPy

1 DefinitionNumPy: fast n-dimensional arrays and maths. pandas: labelled tables (DataFrames) and time series, built on NumPy.
2 CategoryData-processing libraries.
3 WhyTwo years × 3 zones of daily data; shifting, rolling medians and grouping are one-liners.
4 ProblemFeature engineering and evaluation without slow loops.
5 HowOperations run in compiled C over whole columns ("vectorised"). For example, s.shift(7) gives last week's value for every day at once.
6–7 Wheredata.py (synthetic generator), anomaly.py: excess_over_normal(), robust_zscore(), forecast.py: _features_for_series(), build_dataset(), pipeline.py.
8 CommunicationProduces DataFrames → scikit-learn → rows inserted with psycopg2.
9 If removedThe ML would need hundreds of lines of loops.
10 AlternativesPolars (faster), plain Python lists.
11 Pros / cons+ expressive. − memory-hungry for huge data (fine at our size).
12 Viva pointLag features: lag_1, lag_7, lag_14 = litres 1, 7 and 14 days earlier.

scikit-learn

1 DefinitionThe standard Python machine-learning library for classical (non-deep-learning) models.
2 CategoryML library.
3 WhyA uniform fit()/predict() interface, so models are easy to compare fairly.
4 ProblemForecast tomorrow's demand; find unusual days (leaks).
5 How
  • LinearRegression fits a weighted sum of features.
  • RandomForestRegressor averages 300 decision trees, each trained on random samples and features.
  • IsolationForest isolates outliers with random splits: odd points need fewer splits.
6–7 Whereforecast.py: _fit() (RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=3, max_features=0.6, ...)); anomaly.py: isolation_forest().
8 CommunicationTakes pandas features; results written to predictions and model_evaluations.
9 If removedOnly the simple baselines (seasonal naive, moving average) and the robust z-score would remain.
10 Alternativesstatsmodels (ARIMA), Prophet, XGBoost, LSTM (deep learning: needs far more data).
11 Pros / cons+ reliable, simple. − no deep learning (not needed here).
12 Viva point"We split data by time (last 90 days held out), not randomly; otherwise the model would see the future."

matplotlib

1 DefinitionA Python plotting library.
2 CategoryVisualisation library.
3 WhySaves evidence charts for the report.
4 ProblemShowing forecast vs actual and detected leaks.
5 HowBuilds a figure object and renders it to PNG (no screen needed).
6–7 Whereml/jalml/pipeline.py → ml/results/forecast_test.png, leak_detection.png.
8 CommunicationWrites files only. The dashboard draws its own charts in React (SVG), not with matplotlib.
9 If removedNo PNG charts; the app still works.
10 Alternativesseaborn, plotly.
11 Pros / cons+ standard. − static images.
12 Viva pointIt's a reporting tool, not part of the live system.

React 19 (JSX)

1 DefinitionA JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. JSX is HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript.
2 CategoryFrontend UI library.
3 WhyTwo panels with many screens share pieces (header, bell, tables); components make that reuse easy.
4 ProblemKeeping the screen in sync with changing data without manual DOM edits.
5 HowEach component is a function returning UI for its current state (useState). When state changes, React re-runs the function, compares the new virtual DOM with the old one, and updates only what changed. useEffect loads data after rendering.
6–7 Where
  • Root.jsx (sign-in gate: no token → Login; admin → AdminApp; requester → UserApp)
  • Shell.jsx (header, Bell, AccountMenu, useHashTab)
  • Compare.jsx (Allocate tab)
  • Overview.jsx, Forecast.jsx, History.jsx (Records tab), Settings.jsx, Accounts.jsx, Issues.jsx, AuditLog.jsx (inside Compliance in v2.0), Profile.jsx
  • v2.0: Policy.jsx, Supply.jsx (ZoneMap, Timeline, Tankers), FieldData.jsx, Compliance.jsx, Privacy.jsx, NetworkSettings.jsx, i18n.js
  • api.js (all HTTP calls)
8 Communicationfetch() to http://localhost:8000 with Authorization: Bearer.
9 If removedThe API still works (try it at /docs), but there's no friendly UI.
10 AlternativesVue, Angular, Svelte, server-rendered HTML.
11 Pros / cons+ reusable components, huge community. − needs a build step; a big JavaScript download.
12 Viva pointThe UI hides admin tabs from requesters, but security is enforced on the server (role dependencies). Hiding a button is not security.

esbuild (with Node.js)

1 DefinitionA very fast JavaScript bundler/compiler written in Go. Node.js runs the build script.
2 CategoryBuild tool.
3 WhyBrowsers don't understand JSX or import from npm packages directly.
4 ProblemTurns the 27 source files + React into one public/app.js (and app.css).
5 HowFollows imports from main.jsx, converts JSX to function calls, joins everything, minifies.
6–7 Wherefrontend/build.mjs, package.json (npm run build).
8 CommunicationOutput copied by frontend/Dockerfile into nginx.
9 If removedNo rebuilds possible; the committed public/app.js still works.
10 AlternativesVite (uses esbuild inside), webpack.
11 Pros / cons+ builds in about a second. − fewer plugins than webpack.
12 Viva pointThe built file is committed, so Docker doesn't need Node.js on your laptop.

nginx

1 DefinitionA high-performance web server and reverse proxy.
2 CategoryWeb server.
3 WhyServes static files (HTML, JS, CSS) efficiently.
4 ProblemThe browser must download the app from somewhere.
5 HowAn event-driven server: a few worker processes handle thousands of connections, reading files from disk.
6–7 Wherefrontend/Dockerfile (FROM nginx:alpine, copies public/). v1.0 used the default configuration; v2.0 adds nginx.conf.template with security headers (see the v2.0 technologies below). Config
8 CommunicationBrowser → :3000 (mapped to container :80). The page then calls the API directly at :8000; nginx doesn't proxy the API. In the HTTPS profile, Caddy sits in front of both.
9 If removedYou could open the files another way, but there'd be no proper server.
10 AlternativesApache, Caddy (automatic HTTPS), letting FastAPI serve the files.
11 Pros / cons+ tiny image, fast. − no HTTPS by itself (Caddy adds it).
12 Viva pointBecause the page (port 3000) calls the API (port 8000), that's a cross-origin request, so the backend enables CORS.

Docker

1 DefinitionA tool that packages an app with everything it needs into an image, and runs it as an isolated container.
2 CategoryContainerisation / deployment.
3 Why"Works on my machine" problems vanish. Your Windows laptop doesn't need g++, Python packages or PostgreSQL installed.
4 ProblemComplex setup with 4 runtimes.
5 HowUses Linux kernel features: namespaces (each container sees its own processes, network and files) and cgroups (resource limits). On Windows, Docker Desktop runs a small Linux VM (WSL 2). Images are built in layers from Dockerfile steps.
6–7 Wheredb/Dockerfile, backend/Dockerfile (2 stages), ml/Dockerfile, frontend/Dockerfile.
8 CommunicationContainers talk over Compose's private network by service name.
9 If removedManual install of everything.
10 AlternativesPodman, virtual machines, manual installation.
11 Pros / cons+ reproducible, isolated. − uses disk and RAM; Windows needs WSL 2.
12 Viva pointProcess isolation in containers is an OS feature (namespaces) that we use, not implement.

Docker Compose

1 DefinitionA tool that starts several containers together from one YAML file.
2 CategoryContainer orchestration (single machine).
3 WhyOne command: docker compose up --build.
4 ProblemStart order, networking, environment variables, volumes.
5 HowReads docker-compose.yml; builds images; creates the network and the named volume pgdata. A healthcheck (pg_isready) plus depends_on: condition: service_healthy make the backend and ML wait until the DB is ready.
6–7 Wheredocker-compose.yml, .env.example.
8 CommunicationSets DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:jal123@db:5432/jalrakshak for the backend and ML job.
9 If removed4 manual docker run commands.
10 AlternativesKubernetes (multi-machine, much more complex).
11 Pros / cons+ simple. − one machine only.
12 Viva pointThe volume pgdata keeps data between restarts; docker compose down -v deletes it. Schema scripts run only on an empty volume, which is why we built migrate.sql.

GitHub Actions

1 DefinitionGitHub's CI/CD service: it runs scripts on GitHub's machines when you push code.
2 CategoryContinuous integration.
3 WhyEvery change gets tested automatically.
4 ProblemForgetting to run tests.
5 HowThe YAML defines 3 jobs: scheduler (build + test), backend-and-ml (with a PostgreSQL service container), dashboard (npm build).
6–7 Where.github/workflows/ci.yml
8 CommunicationRuns the same test commands you can run locally.
9 If removedTests only run manually.
10 AlternativesGitLab CI, Jenkins.
11 Pros / cons+ free for public repos. − never actually run: the project isn't on GitHub yet.
12 Viva pointSay honestly: "CI is configured; we verified the same commands locally."

PowerShell test script

1 DefinitionPowerShell is Windows' shell and scripting language.
2 CategoryDevelopment tool.
3 WhyYou're on Windows; the script runs all test suites inside Docker containers.
4 ProblemRunning C++/Python/PostgreSQL tests without installing them on Windows.
5 HowCalls docker run with gcc:13 and python:3.12 images and a temporary PostgreSQL.
6–7 Wherescripts/test.ps1
8 CommunicationDocker.
9 If removedManual commands.
10 AlternativesA Makefile, a batch file.
11 Pros / cons+ one command. − not yet run on your laptop.
12 Viva pointShow it running in the demo if possible: it's strong evidence.

Python standard library: OS interfaces and security

1 DefinitionBuilt-in modules:
  • subprocess: start child programs;
  • threading: threads and locks;
  • hashlib/hmac: hashing and safe comparison;
  • secrets: cryptographically secure random numbers.
2 CategoryLibrary over operating-system interfaces.
3 WhyThis is where our code meets the OS: process creation, pipes, mutexes, randomness from the kernel.
4 ProblemRun C++ from Python; protect shared state; store passwords safely.
5 How
  • subprocess.run() asks the kernel to create a child process (on Linux via fork/exec or posix_spawn), connects pipes to its stdin and stdout, writes the input, reads the output, and waits for it to exit.
  • secrets reads from the kernel's random source.
6–7 Where
  • scheduler_client.py: run_scheduler()
  • db.py: _schema_lock = threading.Lock()
  • auth.py: hash_password() (hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac), verify_password() (hmac.compare_digest), _create_session() (secrets.token_urlsafe(32))
8 CommunicationSystem calls into the Linux kernel inside the container.
9 If removedNo scheduler calls and no secure sign-in.
10 Alternativesos.fork/os.pipe directly (lower level), bcrypt/argon2 packages for passwords.
11 Pros / cons+ no extra installs, well reviewed. − PBKDF2 is less memory-hard than Argon2.
12 Viva pointOur code never calls fork() by name. subprocess does it for us, so it's Indirect use of process creation.

HTTP, REST and JSON

1 DefinitionHTTP: the request/response protocol of the web. REST: a style where URLs name resources and methods (GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE) name actions. JSON: a text data format.
2 CategoryProtocol / API style / data format.
3 WhyA universal language between browser and server, and between Python and C++.
4 ProblemDifferent programs need to exchange data.
5 HowThe browser sends POST /me/requests with a JSON body and a token header. The server answers with a status code (201 created, 409 conflict, …) and JSON.
6–7 WhereRoutes in main.py; client in api.js: request(); contract in docs/contracts.md.
8 CommunicationAll tiers.
9 If removed—
10 AlternativesGraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets (for live push).
11 Pros / cons+ simple, debuggable. − no push: the bell re-checks every 30 seconds (setInterval in Shell.jsx), i.e. polling.
12 Viva pointKnow the status codes we use:
  • 400 bad input
  • 401 not signed in
  • 403 wrong role
  • 404 not found (also used to hide other organisations' data)
  • 409 conflict
  • 422 validation
  • 429 locked out, or too many requests (rate limit)
  • 503 database down

Technologies added in v2.0 (12 points each)

v2.0 adds no heavy new framework. Most new features are our own Python and C++ code on top of the same stack. The new technologies are a reverse proxy (Caddy), a hardened nginx configuration, standard-library cryptography for one-time codes, a backup process built on PostgreSQL's own tools, GeoJSON drawn as SVG, and an HTTP device interface. New in v2.0

Caddy (HTTPS reverse proxy)

1 DefinitionA web server that obtains and renews TLS certificates automatically. A reverse proxy receives requests from browsers and forwards them to servers behind it.
2 CategoryWeb server / reverse proxy / TLS terminator.
3 WhyA government system must not send passwords, tokens or 2FA codes in plain text. HTTPS encrypts them in transit.
4 Problem solvedOne HTTPS address for both the web app and the API (/api/...), so there is one origin, no CORS, and HSTS can be sent.
5 How it worksCaddy listens on ports 443 and 80. handle_path /api/* strips /api and forwards to backend:8000 with X-Forwarded-Proto: https. Everything else goes to frontend:80. It answers /config.js itself with apiBase: "/api", so the same built React app works with or without the proxy. With SITE_ADDRESS=localhost it uses its own local certificate authority (tls internal); with a real domain and an admin email it gets a public certificate.
6–7 Whereproxy/Caddyfile, proxy/Dockerfile, service proxy in docker-compose.yml with profiles: ["https"]. Config
8 CommunicationBrowser ⇄ Caddy (TLS) ⇄ nginx / FastAPI (plain HTTP on the private Docker network).
9 If removedThe default setup (ports 3000 and 8000, plain HTTP) still works for a local demo. That's why it is an optional profile: docker compose --profile https up --build.
10 Alternativesnginx + certbot, Traefik, a cloud load balancer that terminates TLS.
11 Pros / cons+ automatic certificates, short config. − one more container; the backend must be told to trust its X-Forwarded-For header (TRUST_PROXY=1) to see real client addresses for rate limiting.
12 Viva point"TLS ends at the proxy; inside the Docker network traffic is plain HTTP, which is normal when the network is private." Honest status: not run in the test environment.

nginx with a Content-Security-Policy (updated)

1 DefinitionCSP is an HTTP header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images and connections the page may use.
2 CategoryWeb server configuration / browser security.
3 WhyIf an attacker ever got text into the page (cross-site scripting, XSS), CSP stops the browser from running injected scripts or sending data elsewhere.
4 Problem solvedDefence in depth for the session token kept in the browser.
5 How it worksThe nginx image fills ${API_ORIGIN} into nginx.conf.template at start-up. The policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' ${API_ORIGIN}; frame-ancestors 'none'; object-src 'none', plus X-Frame-Options: DENY, nosniff, no-referrer and a Permissions-Policy that blocks camera, microphone and location.
6–7 Wherefrontend/nginx.conf.template, frontend/Dockerfile (ENV API_ORIGIN=http://localhost:8000). Config
8 CommunicationThe browser enforces it; nginx only sends it.
9 If removedThe app still works, with less protection.
10 AlternativesSet CSP in a <meta> tag; set it at the proxy.
11 Pros / cons+ strong, cheap. − inline scripts and inline style= attributes in markup break; the React code had to avoid them. The browser walkthrough checked for CSP violations: none.
12 Viva pointWhy is config.js a separate file and not an inline script? Because script-src 'self' forbids inline scripts.

TOTP with the Python standard library (hmac, hashlib, struct, base64, secrets)

1 DefinitionTOTP (Time-based One-Time Password, RFC 6238) makes a 6-digit code from a shared secret and the current 30-second time step. Authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator and others) implement the same standard.
2 CategoryAuthentication algorithm (second factor), implemented with standard-library cryptography.
3 WhyA stolen administrator password alone should not be enough to change who gets water.
4 Problem solvedTwo-factor sign-in without paid SMS gateways or extra Python packages.
5 How it worksSecret: 20 random bytes (secrets.token_bytes) shown as Base32. Code: HMAC-SHA1(secret, counter) where counter = ⌊time ÷ 30⌋ packed as 8 bytes (struct.pack(">Q")); take 4 bytes at an offset given by the last nibble ("dynamic truncation"), mod 106. Verification accepts the previous, current and next step (clock drift) and compares with hmac.compare_digest (constant time).
6–7 Wherebackend/app/mfa.py: new_secret(), code_at(), verify(), begin(), confirm(), disable(); auth.login() and auth.complete_mfa(); Login.jsx: MfaStep; Profile.jsx: MfaPanel. Code
8 CommunicationThe secret is shown once in Profile (and as an otpauth:// link); after that only the 6-digit code travels.
9 If removedSign-in falls back to password only.
10 AlternativesThe pyotp package, SMS OTP, WebAuthn security keys, government SSO (Parichay) with its own 2FA.
11 Pros / cons+ standard, offline, free, ~100 lines. − the secret is stored in the database unencrypted (listed as a limit); a lost phone needs another admin to reset.
12 Viva point"Our server and the phone never talk to each other. Both compute the same HMAC of the same time step from the same secret, so the codes match."

pg_dump backup container

1 Definitionpg_dump is PostgreSQL's tool that writes a consistent copy of one database to a file. pg_restore / psql load it back.
2 CategoryDBMS utility, run by a small long-running container.
3 WhyA department cannot lose its decision records because a disk failed or someone made a mistake.
4 Problem solvedAutomatic daily backups kept for 14 days, and a tested-by-design restore path.
5 How it worksbackup.sh waits for the database (pg_isready), then loops: pg_dump -Fc (compressed custom format) to *.tmp, rename on success (so a half-written file never looks like a backup), delete files older than 14 days (find -mtime), sleep 24 hours. pg_dump uses a snapshot, so the copy is consistent while the app keeps writing.
6–7 Wherebackup/backup.sh, backup/Dockerfile, service backup and volume backups in Compose; scripts/restore.ps1 / restore.sh; the backend mounts the volume read-only to list backups on the Operations page. Config
8 CommunicationConnects to db:5432 over the Docker network.
9 If removedData survives restarts (volume pgdata) but not disk loss or a bad mistake.
10 AlternativesWAL archiving + point-in-time recovery (pgBackRest), a managed database with automated backups, copying the volume.
11 Pros / cons+ simple, standard, restorable on any PostgreSQL. − up to 24 hours of data can be lost (the recovery point); backups are on the same machine unless copied off.
12 Viva point"A backup that has never been restored is only a hope." Honest status: the container and restore scripts were not run in the test environment.

GeoJSON boundaries drawn as SVG

1 DefinitionGeoJSON is a JSON format for map shapes (a Polygon is a list of [longitude, latitude] rings). SVG is the browser's vector-drawing format.
2 CategoryData format + browser graphics.
3 WhyOfficers think in areas of the city; a coloured map shows at a glance which zones are short today.
4 Problem solvedA simple GIS view with no map library and no external tile server (which the CSP would block anyway).
5 How it worksThe backend validates each boundary (network.validate_boundary(): type Polygon/MultiPolygon, closed rings, numeric coordinates within longitude/latitude ranges) and stores it as JSONB in zones.boundary. Supply.jsx: ZoneMap finds the bounding box, scales it into a 600×400 box (flipping y, because latitude grows upwards but SVG y grows downwards), draws each zone as a <path> coloured by whether it meets the norm, and labels the centre with litres per person.
6–7 Wherenetwork.py: validate_boundary(), zone_map(); GET /map/zones; Supply.jsx: ZoneMap, rings(); upload in NetworkSettings.jsx. Code
8 CommunicationJSON over the API; drawn entirely in the browser.
9 If removedThe timetable table still shows everything; only the picture is lost.
10 AlternativesLeaflet / OpenLayers with map tiles, PostGIS for spatial queries, a state GIS portal.
11 Pros / cons+ no dependencies, works offline. − a flat projection (fine for a city), no street background, no spatial queries in SQL.
12 Viva pointDemo boundaries are illustrative polygons, not real ward maps.

Device HTTP interface and the SCADA simulator (urllib)

1 DefinitionSCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems collect readings from field instruments such as reservoir level sensors and flow meters. A gateway forwards those readings to other systems.
2 CategoryIntegration interface (REST endpoint with a per-device key) + a demo client.
3 WhyDecisions should use the real water level and real consumption, not values typed by hand or generated.
4 Problem solvedAny gateway that can make an HTTPS POST can feed JalRakshak.
5 How it worksPOST /telemetry/readings with header X-Device-Key and a JSON list of readings (at most 1,000). The server hashes the key (SHA-256) and looks the device up; only the hash is stored. Readings are inserted with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so resending is harmless. scripts/scada_simulator.py uses only urllib.request to send a slowly falling level and random flows every N seconds.
6–7 Wheretelemetry.py: create_device(), ingest(), _aggregate_day(), import_consumption_csv(), field_alerts(); FieldData.jsx; scripts/scada_simulator.py. Code
8 CommunicationGateway → API → PostgreSQL. No session token: the device key is the credential.
9 If removedStaff enter levels by hand in Settings (the fallback still exists).
10 AlternativesMQTT broker, OPC UA or Modbus gateways, a time-series database such as TimescaleDB.
11 Pros / cons+ simple, idempotent, testable. − real SCADA usually speaks OPC UA/Modbus, so a vendor gateway would be needed; one row per reading would need partitioning at large scale.
12 Viva point"Why hash a device key?" For the same reason as passwords and session tokens: a leaked database must not leak working credentials.

Our own internationalisation (i18n.js)

1 DefinitionInternationalisation (i18n) means the interface can be shown in more than one language.
2 CategoryOur own small library (React context).
3 WhyGIGW (Guidelines for Indian Government Websites) expect bilingual content; many organisation staff prefer Hindi.
4 Problem solvedEnglish / हिंदी switch for sign-in, the whole organisation panel, privacy and 2FA screens, and navigation.
5 How it worksThe English sentence is the key: t("Request water") looks it up in the HI dictionary and falls back to English when there is no entry. {n} placeholders are filled in. The choice is saved per account (PATCH /me/language, column accounts.language) and in the browser before sign-in.
6–7 Wherefrontend/src/i18n.js: LangProvider, useT(); Shell.jsx: LangSwitch; portal.set_language(). Code
8 CommunicationBrowser only, plus one saved setting.
9 If removedEnglish only.
10 Alternativesi18next / react-intl with message IDs and translation files.
11 Pros / cons+ no dependency, code stays readable. − changing an English sentence silently drops its translation; admin screens and server messages are English only (stated in docs/compliance.md). The Hindi text has not been reviewed by a native editor Uncertain.
12 Viva pointAdmin screens being English-only is a deliberate scope limit, not an oversight.

Phase 2 wrap-up

Summary. There are four runtime pieces:

  • browser app (React, served by nginx);
  • API (FastAPI on Uvicorn);
  • scheduler binary (C++);
  • database (PostgreSQL).

There is also a one-shot ML job, and v2.0 adds a backup process and an optional HTTPS proxy. Docker Compose wires them together. v2.0's new features use the same stack plus standard tools: Caddy, a CSP header, standard-library TOTP, pg_dump, GeoJSON/SVG and a device HTTP interface. Each technology has a clear job, and an honest alternative exists for each.

Remember:

  • framework calls you, library is called by you;
  • Uvicorn = server, FastAPI = framework;
  • psycopg2 = driver;
  • Depends() = dependency injection;
  • three validation layers;
  • multi-stage Docker build;
  • CORS because port 3000 ≠ port 8000 (not needed behind Caddy: one origin);
  • CSP forbids inline scripts, hence a separate config.js;
  • TOTP = HMAC of the time step.
1. Why is FastAPI a framework but psycopg2 a library?FastAPI calls our endpoint functions when requests arrive (inversion of control). We call psycopg2's functions ourselves when we want to run SQL.
2. How does the C++ scheduler get into the backend container?Stage 1 of backend/Dockerfile compiles it in gcc:13; COPY --from=scheduler-build puts the binary into the python:3.12-slim image at /usr/local/bin/jalrakshak-scheduler.
3. Name the three validation layers.
  1. Pydantic models in schemas.py.
  2. Business rules in the service code (e.g. at most 5 pending requests, request ≤ capacity).
  3. PostgreSQL CHECK, FK, UNIQUE and NOT NULL constraints.
4. Why does the backend need CORS?The page is served from localhost:3000 but calls localhost:8000. Different ports are different origins, so browsers block the call unless the server allows it (CORSMiddleware, CORS_ORIGINS).
5. What would break if the ML container never ran?Nothing essential. Forecast and leak tabs would be empty, and the scheduler's scarcity factor would use the litres still requested instead of the forecast (_forecast_today() returns None). Allocation still works.

5. How the application starts

docker compose up --build
 1. db        empty volume? run 01_schema.sql, 02_seed.sql, 03_migrate.sql  (else: keep existing data)
              healthcheck: pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 every 3 s -> "healthy" only after the scripts finish
 2. backend   waits for db healthy -> uvicorn starts -> lifespan():
                db.connect(owner=True)  (5 tries, 1 s apart; the schema owner, not the app login)
                db.ensure_schema()      threading.Lock, once per process:
                   migrations.apply()   runs migrate.sql inside BEGIN ... pg_advisory_xact_lock(724001) ... COMMIT
                   ensure_app_role()    lock 724004; CREATE/ALTER ROLE jal_app; GRANT ...; REVOKE ... ON audit_log
                   auth.bootstrap()     lock 724002; if no admin: create admin + 8 demo sign-ins
                   ensure_demo_approver() lock 724003; second admin for maker-checker (demo only)
                migrations.check()      prints "database ready" or what is missing
                privacy.retention()     deletes expired sessions/challenges and data past its retention period
              normal requests then connect as jal_app
              if the DB isn't ready, the API still starts and retries on the first request
 3. ml        waits for db healthy -> pipeline.main(): upgrade_schema() (same migrate.sql) -> generate data
              -> detect leaks -> train/evaluate 4 models -> forecast 7 days -> store() in one transaction -> exit 0
 4. frontend  nginx fills API_ORIGIN into the template, serves public/ on port 3000 with CSP headers
 5. backup    waits for pg_isready, then pg_dump every 24 h (keeps 14 days)
 6. proxy     only with --profile https: Caddy on 443/80 in front of frontend and backend

Backend aur ML job dono ek saath start hote hain aur dono migrate.sql chalate hain. Agar dono ek hi time pe tables banane lagein to clash ho sakta hai. Isliye pg_advisory_xact_lock(724001) lagaya hai: jo pehle pahunchta hai woh upgrade karta hai, doosra wait karta hai, phir sab already bana hua milta hai (IF NOT EXISTS).
