8. Important code sections (A–J format)

Code section 1: the shared simulation engine, run_sequential()

cpp// scheduler/src/sequential.cpp (shortened)
std::vector<Allocation> run_sequential(const Input& in, const Picker& pick) {
    std::vector<bool> done(n, false);
    SeqState st;
    st.clock = initial_clock(in);            // first arrival + batch window
    st.remaining = in.available_litres;
    for (size_t handled = 0; handled < n; ++handled) {
        st.pending_litres = /* sum of litres still asked by not-done requests */;
        std::vector<size_t> ready = collect_ready();     // arrived && !done
        if (ready.empty()) { st.clock = next_arrival; ready = collect_ready(); }  // idle pipeline
        Pick p = pick(ready, st);                        // <-- the only thing that differs per algorithm
        done[p.index] = true;
        double grant = std::min(r.requested_litres, st.remaining);
        if (p.max_grant) grant = std::min(grant, *p.max_grant);          // Water-aware cap
        if (grant <= kEps || grant < min_allocation_ratio * requested) -> "rejected", 0 L
        else { start = st.clock; finish = start + grant / flow_rate_lpm;
               wait = start - arrival; st.remaining -= grant; st.clock = finish; }
    }
}
B Purpose
Simulate one pipeline serving requests one after another, non-preemptively, for any "who goes next" rule.
C Key lines
initial_clock applies the batch window (backend default "all" = wait until the last pending request has arrived). collect_ready is the ready queue. The picker returns an index, a score and an optional cap. grant / flow_rate_lpm is the burst time. A grant smaller than 20% of the request is refused (min_allocation_ratio), so nobody gets a useless trickle.
D Concepts
Discrete-event simulation, ready queue, non-preemptive scheduling, burst time, waiting time = start − arrival, higher-order functions (the picker is a lambda), the strategy pattern.
E Flow
loop n times → compute pending litres → ready set (or jump the clock forward if idle) → pick → grant → advance clock.
F Input / output
In: Input (requests, water, config) + a picker. Out: one Allocation per request (litres, start, finish, wait, status).
G Interaction
Called by FCFS, Priority and Water-aware. Its result goes to execute() for rounding, invariant checks and metrics.
H Why this way
One engine means the comparison is fair: the rules differ only in their choice, not in how time and water are counted.
I If removed / changed
Each algorithm would need its own loop: duplicated, bug-prone code, and results that might not be comparable.
J Improvement
Use a priority queue (heap) for O(n log n) instead of scanning the ready list (O(n²)). Fine at our scale, slow for 100,000 requests.

Code section 2: Water-aware score and guarantee floor

cpp// scheduler/src/water_aware.cpp (core)
const double level = std::min(std::max(demand / left, 0.0), 2.0) / 2.0;   // how scarce, 0..1
const double share = clamp01(r.requested_litres / left);
const double f_priority = r.priority / 5.0;
const double pressure  = 1.0 - clamp01((r.deadline - st.clock) / horizon);
const double f_urgency = 0.5 * (r.urgency / 5.0) + 0.5 * pressure;
const double f_scarcity = level * (1.0 - share);          // scarce water -> favour small requests
const double f_demand = r.zone_population / max_pop;
const double f_fair   = 1.0 - clamp01(r.zone_received_ratio);   // neglected zones first
score = (w.priority*f_priority + w.urgency*f_urgency + w.scarcity*f_scarcity
       + w.demand_impact*f_demand + w.fairness*f_fair) / wsum;
...
// v2.0: each request keeps ITS class's guaranteed share (policy), not one global floor
const double own_floor = floor_share_of(in, chosen) * chosen.requested_litres;   // min_share or 0.3
const double others_floor = std::max(0.0, st.pending_floor_litres - own_floor); // sum of others' shares
const double cap = std::max(own_floor, st.remaining - others_floor);
return Pick{best, best_score, cap};
B Purpose
Our own scheduler: rank by a weighted score, and cap each grant so everyone still waiting keeps its guaranteed share in reserve (30% for every class in policy v1; per class from v2.0).
C Key lines
Every factor is scaled to 0–1, so the weights (0.30/0.25/0.15/0.15/0.15) mean what they say. pressure grows as the deadline approaches (like aging). f_fair uses each zone's past share of committed water (ZONE_RATIO_SQL). Ties go to the earlier arrival, then the lower id, so the result is deterministic.
D Concepts
Multi-criteria priority, dynamic priority (it changes with the clock), starvation prevention, normalisation.
E Flow
For each ready request compute the score → choose the highest → compute the cap → engine grants min(asked, water left, cap).
F Input / output
In: ready list and state. Out: index, score (stored in allocations.score), cap.
G Interaction
Since v2.0 the weights, the default floor and each class's min_share come from the active policy (policy.scheduler_settings()); run_sequential() keeps pending_floor_litres, the sum of the shares still waiting. Predicted demand comes from the ML predictions table.
H Why
Priority alone starves parks and factories; equal shares ignore hospitals. The floor is one knob to move between the two. Experiments: a floor of 0.2 or more removed all zero-water cases.
I If changed
Floor 0 → pure score order (most unequal). Floor 0.5 → nearly equal shares (Jain fairness 1.00 under severe scarcity, importance-weighted 0.50). See experiments/README.md.
J Improvement
Learn or agree the weights with domain experts. (v1.0 listed "make the floor depend on type, e.g. hospitals 50%" here: v2.0 implemented it. Test: "policy class min_share" in C++ and test_class_guaranteed_share_changes_the_plan.)

Code section 3: safety net after every algorithm, execute()

cppOutput execute(const Input& in) {
    std::unique_ptr<Scheduler> s = make_scheduler(in.algorithm);   // factory
    out.allocations = s->run(in);                                  // virtual call
    round_down_to_cents(in, out.allocations);                      // DB stores NUMERIC(12,2)
    check_invariants(in, out.allocations);                         // throws if any rule is broken
    out.remaining_litres = std::max(0.0, in.available_litres - total);
    out.metrics = compute_metrics(in, out.allocations);
}
B Purpose
Run the chosen algorithm, then prove the plan is legal before anyone sees it.
C Key lines
round_down_to_cents floors to 0.01 L, so rounding can never create water. check_invariants verifies:
  • every request appears exactly once;
  • no grant is negative;
  • no grant exceeds its request;
  • the total doesn't exceed the water available.
D Concepts
Polymorphism (virtual run), factory pattern, RAII (unique_ptr frees itself), defensive programming, invariants.
E Flow
factory → run → round → check → metrics → JSON.
F Input / output
Input → Output (plan, remaining litres, metrics).
G Interaction
Called by main(). A thrown exception becomes {"error": …} with exit code 1 → Python SchedulerError → HTTP 400, and the transaction rolls back.
H Why
Two layers of protection: the C++ checks, then the DB CHECK. A fuzz test runs 1,200 random inputs through all algorithms and checks the invariants.
I If removed
Floating-point error could make the total slightly larger than the available water, and the DB would reject it with a confusing error.
J Improvement
Use integer centilitres throughout to avoid floating point entirely.

Code section 4: calling the scheduler as a child process

python# backend/app/scheduler_client.py
def run_scheduler(payload, binary=None, timeout=None):
    binary = binary or config.SCHEDULER_BIN
    timeout = timeout or config.SCHEDULER_TIMEOUT_S            # 10 s
    try:
        proc = subprocess.run([binary], input=json.dumps(payload), capture_output=True,
                              text=True, timeout=timeout)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        raise SchedulerUnavailable(f"scheduler binary not found: {binary}")
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        raise SchedulerUnavailable(f"scheduler timed out after {timeout}s")
    data = json.loads(proc.stdout)       # (JSONDecodeError -> SchedulerUnavailable)
    if proc.returncode != 0:
        raise SchedulerError(data.get("error", "scheduler failed"))
    return data
B Purpose
Run the C++ program and exchange JSON with it.
C Key lines
subprocess.run([binary], ...) creates a child process (a list of arguments, no shell, so no shell injection). input= writes to its stdin pipe. capture_output=True creates pipes for stdout and stderr. timeout kills a hung child. returncode is the exit status the parent collects (like wait()).
D Concepts
Process creation, parent/child, IPC through pipes, exit codes, timeouts, process termination.
E Flow
serialise → spawn → write stdin → child computes → read stdout → child exits → check code → parse.
F Input / output
dict → dict, or one of two exceptions.
G Interaction
Called by service._plan(), from both simulate and commit.
H Why
Language-independent and crash-isolated: if the C++ crashes, only the child dies, never the API. Simple to test from the command line (scheduler < sample_input.json).
I If changed
Without the timeout, a stuck scheduler would hold DB row locks forever. Using shell=True would add injection risk.
J Improvement
Start-up cost (a few ms per process) could be removed with a long-running scheduler service, or a Python extension module (pybind11).

Code section 5: the critical transaction, commit_allocation()

Shown in its v1.0 form for clarity. v2.0 adds, inside the same locked transaction, the policy context, the officer override, the comparison of all rules, and the new columns of scheduler_runs (code section 11).

pythondef commit_allocation(conn, reservoir_id, algorithm, actor=None):
    with conn:                                       # BEGIN ... COMMIT, or ROLLBACK on any exception
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute("SELECT reservoir_id, available_litres FROM reservoirs "
                        "WHERE reservoir_id = %s FOR UPDATE", (reservoir_id,))      # lock #1
            reservoir = cur.fetchone()
            pending = _fetch_pending(cur, reservoir_id, lock=True)   # ... FOR UPDATE OF r  (lock #2)
            if not pending:
                raise ConflictError("no pending requests for this reservoir")       # -> 409
            result = _plan(cur, algorithm, reservoir["available_litres"], pending)  # C++ child process
            total = sum(Decimal(str(a["allocated_litres"])) for a in result["allocations"])
            INSERT INTO scheduler_runs (...) RETURNING run_id
            for a in allocations: INSERT INTO allocations ...; UPDATE water_requests SET status = ...
            UPDATE reservoirs SET available_litres = available_litres - total ...
            for a in allocations: audit.notify_organisation(...)       # same transaction
            audit.write(cur, actor, "plan.apply", "run", run_id, {...})
B Purpose
Apply one plan exactly once, completely or not at all.
C Key lines
with conn: is the transaction boundary. FOR UPDATE makes a second operator's transaction wait at lock #1 until the first commits. It then sees no pending requests → 409. Decimal avoids floating-point error in the subtraction. Notifications and audit go in the same transaction.
D Concepts
ACID, critical section, mutual exclusion, exclusive row locks, lock ordering (deadlock prevention), RETURNING, atomic notification ("outbox"-style).
E Flow
lock reservoir → lock requests → plan → write 6 kinds of rows → commit (locks released).
F Input / output
reservoir id, algorithm, actor → plan + run_id. Errors: 404, 409, 400, 500.
G Interaction
scheduler_client, audit, PostgreSQL. The frontend re-loads status afterwards.
H Why
Without locks, two clicks at the same moment both see "50,000 L and 8 pending" and both save plans. The demo showed 160,000 L handed out for 80,000 L of requests.
I If removed
See the concurrency demo: double allocation. The CHECK constraint catches only cases where the level would go below 0.
J Improvement
Run the C++ before taking locks and re-check afterwards (optimistic approach) to shorten lock time; add a request id to make retries safe (idempotency).

Code section 6: sign-in with lockout, auth.login()

pythoncur.execute("SELECT account_id, email, password_hash, status, failed_logins, locked_until, "
            "locked_until > now() AS locked, ... FROM accounts WHERE lower(email) = %s FOR UPDATE", (email,))
acc = cur.fetchone()
if acc is None:
    verify_password(password or "", _dummy_hash())        # same time cost for unknown emails
    result = ("fail", None)
elif acc["locked"]:
    result = ("locked", minutes_left)
elif not verify_password(password or "", acc["password_hash"]):
    failed = acc["failed_logins"] + 1
    if failed >= config.MAX_FAILED_LOGINS:                 # 5
        UPDATE accounts SET failed_logins = 0, locked_until = now() + 5 minutes
    ...
else:
    UPDATE accounts SET failed_logins = 0, locked_until = NULL, last_login_at = now()
    token, expires = _create_session(cur, acc["account_id"])     # secrets.token_urlsafe(32), store sha256
B Purpose
Check a password safely and resist guessing.
C Key lines
  • FOR UPDATE: two parallel wrong guesses can't both read "4 failures" and skip the lock (a race condition otherwise).
  • Dummy hash: an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password, so attackers can't discover which emails exist.
  • The same message, "wrong email or password", in both cases.
D Concepts
Hashing with salt, key stretching, constant-time comparison, row locks protecting a counter (critical section), timing side channel.
E Flow
normalise email → lock row → branch → audit → commit → raise the right error or return the token.
F Input / output
email, password → {token, expires_at, account} or 401/403/429.
G Interaction
account_for_token() is used by every protected endpoint afterwards.
H Why
Standard practice (OWASP), and every piece can be explained.
I If removed
Unlimited guessing; plain-text tokens in the DB would be usable by anyone who reads the database.
J Improvement
Argon2id, email password reset. (Rate limiting per IP address and two-factor sign-in were added in v2.0: code sections 14 and 15.)

Code section 7: authorisation as dependencies

pythondef current_account(authorization: Optional[str] = Header(default=None), conn=Depends(get_conn)):
    return auth.account_for_token(conn, _bearer(authorization))     # 401 if missing/expired

def admin_account(me=Depends(current_account)):
    if me["role"] != "admin":
        raise Forbidden("this needs an administrator account")      # 403
    return me

@app.post("/allocate/commit")
def commit(body: CommitBody, me=Depends(admin_account), conn=Depends(get_conn)): ...
B Purpose
Decide who may call each endpoint, in one reusable place.
C Key lines
The token from the header is hashed with SHA-256 and looked up in sessions joined with accounts, where expires_at > now(). An inactive account has its sessions deleted. v2.0: admin_account() also refuses an admin without 2FA when REQUIRE_ADMIN_MFA=1.
D Concepts
Authentication (who are you) vs authorisation (what may you do), role-based access control (RBAC), dependency injection.
E Flow
get_conn → current_account → role check → endpoint.
F Input / output
header → account dict, or 401/403.
G Interaction
Used by 88 of the 95 routes. The 7 others: /health, GET /zones, /auth/login, /auth/register, /auth/mfa (needs the sign-in challenge), /privacy-notice, and /telemetry/readings (needs a device key instead). portal.py additionally filters by the caller's own organisation (and returns 404 for other organisations' data).
H Why
One rule in one place is hard to forget.
I If removed
Anyone could apply plans or read others' data. Tested in test_operations_need_an_admin_session and test_requester_sees_and_changes_only_their_own_requests.
J Improvement
Finer permissions (e.g. "viewer" admins); cache session lookups.

Code section 8: self-upgrading database, ensure_schema()

python_schema_ready = False
_schema_lock = threading.Lock()
def ensure_schema(conn):
    global _schema_ready
    if _schema_ready:                 # fast path, no lock
        return
    with _schema_lock:                # only one thread upgrades
        if _schema_ready:             # re-check (double-checked locking)
            return
        migrations.apply(conn)        # migrate.sql: BEGIN; pg_advisory_xact_lock(724001); ... COMMIT
        auth.bootstrap(conn)
        _schema_ready = True
B Purpose
Bring an old database up to date automatically, exactly once per process.
C Key lines
A Python mutex stops two threads in the same process. The advisory lock stops two processes (backend + ML job). The check-lock-recheck pattern avoids taking the lock on every request.
D Concepts
Mutex, critical section, double-checked locking, idempotent migration, process-level vs thread-level synchronisation.
E Flow
First request (or start-up) → upgrade → mark ready → later calls return immediately.
F Input / output
connection → none (raises DatabaseUnavailable with advice).
G Interaction
Called by get_conn() and lifespan().
H Why
Your real error in v0.4 (relation "model_evaluations" does not exist) came from an old Docker volume. Now it fixes itself.
I If removed
Old volumes break the app until docker compose down -v.
J Improvement
A migration tool with numbered versions (Alembic, Flyway).

Code section 10: the zone supply timetable, build_timetable() v2.0

cpp// scheduler/src/timetable.cpp (shortened). Per source:
// ---- 1. HOW MUCH each zone gets today
const double budget = std::min(s.release_litres, s.pump_capacity_lph * hours);
for (size_t i : members) {                        // zones fed by this source
    target.push_back(z.target);                   // min(demand, inlet_capacity * hours)
    total_floor += z.min_share * z.target;
    weight.push_back(z.priority * (1.0 - z.min_share) * z.target);
}
if (total_target <= budget)        given = target;                         // enough for everyone
else if (total_floor >= budget)    given[k] = floor_k * budget / total_floor;  // not even floors fit: scale
else { given[k] = floor_k;  water_fill(given, target, weight, budget - total_floor); }
allocated = std::floor(given + 1e-6);             // whole litres, never more

// ---- 2. WHEN: hourly slots of pump capacity, most important zone first
std::vector<double> free(nslots, std::floor(s.pump_capacity_lph * slot_h));
stable_sort(order, by priority desc, then zone_id);
for (zone : order) {
    rate = floor(inlet_capacity_lph * slot_h);          // litres per slot through the zone's main
    k = ceil(allocated / rate);                         // slots needed
    start = earliest j such that slots j..j+k-1 each have free[t] >= amount;   // one continuous block
    if (no such j) split: take whatever is free, earliest first;
    free[t] -= put[t];  join neighbouring slots into blocks "05:00-11:00"
}
// ---- invariants: source never releases more than available; no slot over pump capacity;
//      no zone above its demand. Any violation -> exception -> exit code 1.
cpp// Weighted water-filling: share `budget` in proportion to weight, but never above a zone's room.
while (budget - spent > 1e-6) {
    wsum = sum of weight[i] over active zones;
    for each active zone i:
        if (pool * weight[i] / wsum >= room_i) { given[i] += room_i; spent += room_i; active[i] = false; capped = true; }
    if (capped) continue;                    // someone filled up: recompute shares for the rest
    for each active zone i: given[i] += pool * weight[i] / wsum;   // nobody is full: final split
    break;
}
B Purpose
Turn "the reservoir releases X litres today" into "zone A gets water 05:00–11:00, zone B 11:00–18:00…", within every physical limit.
C Key lines
target = min(demand, inlet × hours): a zone can never take more than its main carries in the supply window. The floors are the zone's guaranteed share (zone_min_share from the policy, 30% in v1). Water-filling fills zones like containers: a zone that would receive more than it needs is capped and the leftover is shared again among the others. std::floor keeps whole litres and can only round down. In the placement step, free[t] is the pump capacity left in slot t.
D Concepts
Resource allocation with guarantees (like a minimum CPU share), proportional sharing, the water-filling algorithm (the same idea is used to share bandwidth or power in networking), slot scheduling / bin packing with a greedy first-fit rule, invariants. Complexity: water-filling at most n rounds of O(n) → O(n²); placement O(n · slots²) in the worst case.
E Flow
parse + validate → per source: budget → floors → water-fill → place in slots → check invariants → metrics (served ratio, minimum L/person, zones below norm, Jain fairness between zones) → JSON.
F Input / output
In: {"mode":"timetable","lpcd":135,"day_start_hour":5,"day_end_hour":23,"slot_minutes":60,"sources":[…],"zones":[…]}. Out: per zone demand, delivered, litres per person, meets_norm, hours and blocks; per source delivered litres and pump use; overall metrics.
G Interaction
network.build_draft() builds the input from the DB (scheduler_client.build_timetable_input(), policy norm and shares, today's release per source, metered demand if chosen), stores input and result in supply_timetables as a draft. publish() and plan_tankers() read the stored result.
H Why this way
Separating how much from when keeps each step simple and testable. Priority decides who is placed first (gets the earliest hours and the extra water), the floors stop a low-priority zone from getting nothing, and the same C++ binary and invariant style as the allocation rules is reused.
I If changed
Without floors, a high-priority zone could take everything in a drought. Without the inlet cap, the plan could promise water a pipe cannot carry. Without the "continuous block" search, a zone could get water in many scattered hours, which residents can't plan around.
J Improvement
Fair rotation of who gets the convenient morning hours across days; minimum and maximum hours per zone; pressure/hydraulic limits from a network model (EPANET); an exact optimiser (linear programming) instead of a greedy placement.

Code section 11: officer override, _apply_overrides() and the manual mode v2.0

python# backend/app/service.py (inside commit_allocation, after the reservoir and requests are locked)
context = _context(cur)                                    # active policy, zone ratios, forecast
base = _plan(cur, algorithm, available, pending, context=context)
fixed, changes = _apply_overrides(base, pending, overrides, reason, available)
if fixed is not None:                                      # the officer changed some litres
    order = {a["request_id"]: i for i, a in enumerate(base["allocations"])}
    ordered = sorted(pending, key=lambda r: order[r["request_id"]])   # keep the edited plan's order
    result = _plan(cur, "manual", available, ordered, fixed_litres=fixed, context=context)
comparison = _comparison(cur, algorithm, available, pending, context, base)   # metrics of all 4 rules

# ... audit "plan.apply" and, if changed, "plan.override" {reason, changes}

def _apply_overrides(base, pending, overrides, reason, available):
    if len(reason.strip()) < config.OVERRIDE_REASON_MIN_CHARS:            # 10
        raise InvalidInput("changing a plan needs a reason of at least 10 characters ...")
    for rid, litres in overrides.items():
        if rid not in pending ids: raise InvalidInput(...)
        if litres < 0 or litres > asked: raise InvalidInput(...)
        if litres != plan litres: changes.append({"request_id", "plan_litres", "final_litres"})
    if sum(fixed) > available: raise InvalidInput("... gives out more than is available")
cpp// scheduler/src/manual.cpp: serve in the given order, exactly fixed_litres each
in.config.min_allocation_ratio = 0;                   // the officer's decision stands, even small amounts
if (total fixed > in.available_litres) throw std::runtime_error("manual plan gives out more water than is available");
return run_sequential(in, [&](const std::vector<size_t>& ready, const SeqState&) {
    size_t best = smallest index in ready;           // input order
    return Pick{best, std::nullopt, *in.requests[best].fixed_litres};
});
B Purpose
Let a human change the recommendation, but never silently: the reason, the before/after litres, the policy and the alternatives are stored with the run.
C Key lines
The edited plan goes back through the same engine as a fifth "rule" (manual), so waits, fairness and invariant checks are computed exactly like the others. _comparison() runs the other three rules on the same locked data and stores their metrics in scheduler_runs.comparison (JSONB).
D Concepts
Human-in-the-loop decision support, validation at two layers (Python, then C++), the strategy pattern again (one more picker), accountability / non-repudiation via the audit log.
E Flow
lock → plan with the chosen rule → validate edits → manual re-run → comparison → write run, allocations, notifications ("set by the officer"), two audit rows → commit.
F Input / output
POST /allocate/commit {"algorithm":"priority","overrides":{"6":2000,"8":5000},"reason":"…"} → the final plan with run_id and the list of changes.
G Interaction
Compare.jsx: OverridePanel; report.run_report_html()/csv() print the decision record from the stored run.
H Why
A department will not accept a system that forbids judgement, nor one where judgement leaves no trace. Both are met.
I If removed
Officers would apply a plan and fix it outside the system, so the records would be wrong.
J Improvement
Run the comparison before taking the locks (it costs three extra scheduler processes while rows are locked); require a second approval for overrides above some size.

Code section 12: maker-checker approval, policy.decide() v2.0

pythondef decide(conn, actor, policy_id, approve, note=None):
    with conn:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute("SELECT * FROM policies WHERE policy_id = %s FOR UPDATE", (policy_id,))
            p = cur.fetchone()
            if p["status"] != "pending":
                raise ConflictError("only a policy waiting for approval can be approved or rejected")
            if p["proposed_by"] == actor["account_id"] and config.REQUIRE_SECOND_APPROVER:
                raise Forbidden("maker-checker: a policy must be approved by a different administrator ...")
            if not approve:
                if not note: raise InvalidInput("give a reason for rejecting the policy")
                UPDATE policies SET status = 'rejected', decided_by, decided_at, decision_note ...
                return
            # lock the active policy too, so two approvals cannot both activate
            cur.execute("SELECT policy_id FROM policies WHERE status = 'approved' FOR UPDATE")
            cur.execute("UPDATE policies SET status = 'superseded' WHERE status = 'approved'")
            cur.execute("UPDATE policies SET status = 'approved', decided_by = %s, ... WHERE policy_id = %s", ...)
            changed = apply_class_priorities(cur, p)    # organisations without a manual exception
            audit.write(cur, actor, "policy.approve", ...); audit.notify_admins(...)
sql-- db/migrate.sql: at most ONE approved policy, enforced by the database itself
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS policies_one_active ON policies ((TRUE)) WHERE status = 'approved';
B Purpose
Make a policy change a two-person decision, and switch the active policy atomically.
C Key lines
The proposer check compares account ids, not names. Locking both the pending row and the currently approved row serialises two approvals happening at once. The partial unique index indexes the constant TRUE only for approved rows, so a second approved row would be a duplicate key: even buggy code could not create two active policies.
D Concepts
Separation of duties (maker-checker, "four-eyes principle"), state machine (draft → pending → approved / rejected → superseded), mutual exclusion with row locks, a database constraint as the last line of defence.
E Flow
lock pending → checks → (reject with reason) or (lock active → supersede → approve → update priorities → audit → notify) → commit.
F Input / output
POST /admin/policies/{id}/decide {"approve": true, "note": "…"} → the policy as now stored. Errors 403 (same person), 409 (not pending), 400 (no reason).
G Interaction
policy.scheduler_settings() feeds every plan and timetable from the active policy; the run stores policy_id.
H Why
Government financial and operational rules commonly require a second officer for changes that affect many people. The demo has a second admin for this reason.
I If changed
REQUIRE_SECOND_APPROVER=0 allows self-approval for a one-person installation; the audit row then records "self_approved": true.
J Improvement
Effective dates (approve now, activate on the 1st), attaching the scanned government order, different approval levels per field.

Code section 13: sensor readings, telemetry.ingest() v2.0

pythondef ingest(conn, device_key, readings):
    # validate first, outside the transaction: values numeric and >= 0, at most 1000, times parsed
    parsed.sort()
    with conn:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute("SELECT device_id, kind, reservoir_id, zone_id, active, name FROM devices "
                        "WHERE key_hash = %s FOR UPDATE", (_hash(device_key),))     # sha256 of the key
            dev = cur.fetchone()
            if dev is None or not dev["active"]:
                raise NotSignedIn("unknown or disabled device key")                 # 401
            for t, v in parsed:
                cur.execute("INSERT INTO readings (device_id, measured_at, value) VALUES (%s, %s, %s) "
                            "ON CONFLICT (device_id, measured_at) DO NOTHING RETURNING reading_id", ...)
            UPDATE devices SET last_seen_at = now(), last_value = ...
            if dev["kind"] == "reservoir_level":
                cur.execute("SELECT capacity_litres FROM reservoirs WHERE reservoir_id = %s FOR UPDATE", ...)
                if last_v > cap: raise InvalidInput("... above the reservoir capacity (check the sensor calibration)")
                UPDATE reservoirs SET available_litres = last_v ...
                audit.write(cur, {"account_id": None, "email": f"device:{dev['name']}"}, "telemetry.level", ...)
            if dev["kind"] == "zone_flow":
                for d in days: _aggregate_day(cur, zone_id, d)   # consumption(zone, day) = SUM(readings), source 'meter'
B Purpose
Accept field readings safely and turn them into the numbers the planners use.
C Key lines
Hash lookup (the key itself is never stored). ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes a resend harmless (idempotent). The reservoir row is locked with FOR UPDATE, the same lock that commit_allocation() takes first, so a level update and a plan commit can never interleave. A level above capacity is refused with a calibration hint, and the whole batch rolls back.
D Concepts
Authentication of machines, idempotency, upsert (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE in _aggregate_day), aggregation with SUM, critical section shared with another operation, audit of non-human actors.
E Flow
validate → lock device → insert readings → update device → (lock reservoir → set level → audit) or (aggregate days) → commit.
F Input / output
X-Device-Key + {"readings":[{"measured_at":"…","value":30237}]} → {"stored": n, "duplicates": m, "reservoir_level": …}.
G Interaction
field_alerts() reports devices silent for 30 minutes; the ML job reads consumption rows with source meter; the timetable can use metered demand.
H Why
Gateways resend after network errors; field sensors drift. Both cases are handled without corrupting data.
I If changed
Without the reservoir lock, a sensor update arriving during a commit could overwrite the level the commit just reduced (a lost update).
J Improvement
Plausibility checks (rate of change), per-device rate limits, a time-series store for millions of readings.

Code section 14: two-factor codes, mfa.code_at() / verify() and auth.complete_mfa() v2.0

pythonSTEP, DIGITS, WINDOW = 30, 6, 1

def code_at(secret, counter):
    digest = hmac.new(_key(secret), struct.pack(">Q", counter), hashlib.sha1).digest()
    offset = digest[-1] & 0x0F                                   # dynamic truncation (RFC 4226)
    value = struct.unpack(">I", digest[offset:offset + 4])[0] & 0x7FFFFFFF
    return str(value % 10 ** DIGITS).zfill(DIGITS)

def verify(secret, code, now=None):
    counter = int((now if now is not None else time.time()) // STEP)
    return any(hmac.compare_digest(code_at(secret, counter + d), code) for d in range(-WINDOW, WINDOW + 1))

# auth.complete_mfa(): second step of sign-in
SELECT c.account_id, c.attempts, c.expires_at > now() AS valid, a.mfa_secret ...
  FROM login_challenges c JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = c.account_id
 WHERE c.token_hash = %s FOR UPDATE OF c
if not valid or attempts >= 5: DELETE challenge -> "start again"
elif not mfa.verify(secret, code): UPDATE login_challenges SET attempts = attempts + 1; audit "login.mfa_failed"
else: DELETE challenge; create the real session; audit "login" {"mfa": true}
B Purpose
A second factor: something you have (the phone) besides something you know (the password).
C Key lines
After a correct password, login() does not create a session for an account with 2FA; it creates a short-lived challenge (5 minutes, stored hashed). Only POST /auth/mfa with the challenge and a valid code creates the session. Attempts are counted under a row lock, so parallel guesses can't exceed 5.
D Concepts
HMAC, time as a shared counter, clock drift window, constant-time comparison (timing side channel), a two-step state machine, row lock protecting a counter.
E Flow
password OK → challenge → code → verify → session.
F Input / output
{"challenge": "…", "code": "123456"} → {token, account} or 401.
G Interaction
admin_account() refuses admins without 2FA when REQUIRE_ADMIN_MFA=1; admin_service.reset_mfa() lets another admin reset a lost phone (audited).
H Why
Standard, offline, and verifiable in a test (test_two_factor_sign_in computes real codes).
I If changed
A window of 0 would reject codes from phones whose clocks are a few seconds off; a large window makes guessing easier.
J Improvement
Encrypt mfa_secret with a key kept outside the database; block reuse of the same code within its window; recovery codes.

Code section 15: the rate limiter, security.RateLimiter v2.0

pythonclass RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self):
        self._hits = defaultdict(deque)     # (client address, bucket) -> times of recent requests
        self._lock = threading.Lock()       # FastAPI runs requests on several threads

    def allow(self, key, limit, now=None):
        now = time.monotonic() if now is None else now
        with self._lock:
            q = self._hits[key]
            while q and q[0] <= now - 60:   # forget hits older than one minute (sliding window)
                q.popleft()
            if len(q) >= limit:
                return False                # -> 429 "too many requests", Retry-After: 60
            q.append(now)
            return True
# main.py middleware: bucket "auth" (/auth/...) 20 per minute, "api" 600 per minute, /health free
B Purpose
Slow down password guessing and floods from one address.
C Key lines
A deque per client is a queue of timestamps: old ones leave from the left, new ones join on the right. time.monotonic() never jumps backwards when the system clock is changed. The threading.Lock makes "check then append" one atomic step.
D Concepts
Mutex and critical section (in our own Python code), race condition (two threads both seeing 19 hits and both passing), sliding-window algorithm, monotonic clock.
E Flow
middleware → bucket by path → allow() → 429 or continue → add security headers.
F Input / output
(address, bucket), limit → True / False.
G Interaction
client_address() uses X-Forwarded-For only when TRUST_PROXY=1 (behind Caddy), otherwise anyone could fake their address.
H Why
Account lockout protects one account; the rate limit protects against trying many accounts.
I If changed
Without the lock, the counter can be exceeded under parallel requests.
J Improvement
The counters live in one process's memory: with several API processes or servers, store them in Redis.

Code section 16: least-privilege database login, migrations.ensure_app_role() v2.0

pythoncur.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(724004) AS locked")
cur.execute("SELECT 1 AS x FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = %s", (user,))
verb = "ALTER" if cur.fetchone() else "CREATE"
# format() quotes the name (%I) and the password (%L) safely on the server
cur.execute(f"SELECT format('{verb} ROLE %%I WITH LOGIN PASSWORD %%L', %s::text, %s::text) AS sql", (user, password))
cur.execute(cur.fetchone()["sql"])
for stmt in ("GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE %I TO %I", "GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO %I",
             "GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO %I",
             "GRANT USAGE, SELECT ON ALL SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA public TO %I",
             "REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE ON audit_log FROM %I",
             "REVOKE TRUNCATE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public FROM %I"):
    ... format(stmt, user) on the server, then execute the result
B Purpose
The running API should hold only the rights it needs. If it were ever tricked into running bad SQL, it still could not drop tables or rewrite history.
C Key lines
DDL and role names can't be passed as %s parameters, so the statement text is built by PostgreSQL's own format() with %I (identifier quoting) and %L (literal quoting). Run on every start, so tables added by later versions are granted too. The advisory lock 724004 stops two processes creating the role at once.
D Concepts
DCL (GRANT/REVOKE), principle of least privilege, defence in depth (REVOKE + two triggers on the audit log), safe dynamic SQL.
E Flow
owner connection → lock → create/alter role → grants → revokes → commit; db.connect() then logs in as jal_app for normal requests.
F Input / output
APP_DB_USER, APP_DB_PASSWORD → True (or False when not configured).
G Interaction
db.ensure_schema() (owner connection) → migrations → this → bootstrap; the Operations page shows whether the restricted user is in use.
H Why
In v1.0 the app connected as the postgres superuser, which can do anything, including disabling triggers.
I If removed
Everything still works, with a larger blast radius.
J Improvement
Separate read-only role for reports; row-level security per organisation; secrets from a vault instead of environment variables.

10. Error handling and validation

  • Exception → HTTP mapping in main.py:
    • NotFound → 404
    • Conflict → 409
    • InvalidInput → 400
    • NotSignedIn → 401 (with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer)
    • Forbidden → 403
    • TooManyAttempts → 429 (rate limiting answers 429 from the middleware, with Retry-After: 60)
    • SchedulerError → 400
    • SchedulerUnavailable → 500
    • DatabaseUnavailable / OperationalError → 503
    • other psycopg2 errors → 500 with the PostgreSQL code, plus an "older database" hint for 42P01/42883/42703
  • PostgreSQL error codes translated (service._db_errors):
    • 23505 unique → "another … already has that name";
    • 23503 foreign key → "still in use";
    • 23514 check → "breaks a database rule".
  • Transactions guarantee that a failure leaves no half-written data (tested: test_failed_commit_leaves_the_database_untouched, test_failed_scheduler_rolls_back_without_writes).
  • Frontend shows detail text in toasts; a 401 sends you back to sign-in.
  • C++ validates input in model_io.cpp and checks invariants after every run.

Phase 3 wrap-up

Summary. The code is layered: routes → services → helpers, with the C++ as an isolated computation. The important code is:

  • run_sequential and the pickers;
  • execute with invariants;
  • run_scheduler (child process);
  • commit_allocation (locked transaction);
  • auth.login;
  • role dependencies;
  • ensure_schema;
  • v2.0: build_timetable, _apply_overrides + manual, policy.decide, telemetry.ingest, TOTP, RateLimiter, ensure_app_role.

Remember:

  • entry points (API, scheduler, ML job, web app, DB init; v2.0 adds backup loop, proxy, simulator);
  • start-up order guarded by the healthcheck;
  • two lock levels (thread mutex + DB advisory lock), now 4 advisory locks;
  • owner login for upgrades, jal_app for requests;
  • exception → status-code table;
  • the honest weaknesses list.
1. What is the only difference between FCFS, Priority and Water-aware in code?The picker lambda passed to run_sequential(). FCFS picks the earliest arrival, Priority the highest priority, Water-aware the highest score (and also returns a cap).
2. What happens if the C++ finds an invariant broken during a commit?It prints {"error": …} and exits with code 1. Python raises SchedulerError; the with conn: block rolls back; the user gets HTTP 400; nothing is saved.
3. Why both threading.Lock and pg_advisory_xact_lock?The Python lock synchronises threads inside one backend process. The advisory lock synchronises separate processes (backend and ML job) that both run migrate.sql.
4. Where is the role check for /allocate/commit?In the dependency me=Depends(admin_account) in main.py. admin_account depends on current_account, which validates the token.
4b. In a commit with an override, how many times does the scheduler run, and why?Up to five: once for the chosen rule (the plan the officer edited), three times for the other rules (the stored comparison), and once in manual mode for the edited plan, so its timing and metrics are computed by the same engine.
5. Name one real weakness and its fix.Example: there is no connection pool, so every request opens a new DB connection. Fix: psycopg2.pool.ThreadedConnectionPool or PgBouncer. (Others: the hard-coded reservoir id 1, the duplicated SQL function, polling.)

Phase 4 · Operating Systems concepts: deep dive

The golden rule for your viva. Separate three things:

  1. Our code explicitly implements an OS algorithm. Example: FCFS / Priority / Round Robin as a simulation of water delivery in C++. Explicit
  2. Our code asks the OS to do something. Example: create a child process, open pipes, create threads. Indirect
  3. Our program merely runs on an OS, which does paging, CPU scheduling of real processes, and so on. Theoretical, since we don't implement or control it.

Never say "our project implements paging". Say: "it runs on Linux, which uses paging; we didn't implement memory management."

A. Process management

Program vs process Indirect

1 Definition
A program is a file of instructions on disk (/usr/local/bin/jalrakshak-scheduler). A process is a program while it is running: it has memory, open files, a process ID (PID) and a state.
2 Why needed
The OS must track each running instance separately. Two admins clicking "Compare" at the same moment start two separate scheduler processes from the same program file.
3 Internals
The kernel creates a process structure (the PCB), gives it a virtual address space, loads the code, sets up file descriptors 0/1/2 and puts it in the ready queue.
4 In our project
The backend (Uvicorn/Python) is one long-running process. Each scheduler run is a short-lived child process. PostgreSQL runs one server process per client connection. Each Docker container's main program is PID 1 inside its namespace.
5 Where
scheduler_client.run_scheduler(); backend/Dockerfile CMD.
6 Example
Simulate with 4 algorithms → _plan() is called 4 times → 4 child processes are created one after another, each living a few milliseconds.
7 Analogy
A recipe book (program) vs a cook actually cooking from it (process). Four cooks can follow the same recipe at once.
9 Pros / limits
+ isolation: a crash in the C++ can't corrupt the API. − creating a process costs time (milliseconds).
10 Viva
Q: Is the scheduler a thread or a process? A: A separate process, created by subprocess.run for each run. It shares no memory with the API and talks only through pipes.

Process creation, parent/child, termination, PID/PPID Indirect

  Uvicorn worker (Python)  PID e.g. 1        (parent)
        |  subprocess.run(["jalrakshak-scheduler"], input=..., timeout=10)
        |     -> kernel: create child (fork+exec or posix_spawn), pipes for fds 0,1,2
        v
  jalrakshak-scheduler     PID e.g. 57, PPID = 1   (child)
        reads fd 0 (stdin) ... computes ... writes fd 1 (stdout)
        return 0 / return 1  -> exit status
        |
  parent waits (like wait()/waitpid()) -> collects exit status -> proc.returncode
  if 10 s pass first: parent kills the child (TimeoutExpired) -> SchedulerUnavailable
1 Definition
Process creation: a running process asks the kernel to start a new one, its child. The child gets its own PID; its PPID is the parent's PID. Termination: the child calls exit (here: return from main), and the parent waits to collect the exit status. Otherwise the child becomes a "zombie" until it is collected.
2 Why
So programs can run other programs, even ones written in other languages.
3 Internals
Classic Unix: fork() copies the parent (copy-on-write memory), then exec() replaces the copy's code with the new program, and the parent calls wait(). Python's subprocess uses fork/exec or posix_spawn internally. We don't call these by name.
4–5 Ours
backend/app/scheduler_client.py, lines around subprocess.run([binary], input=json.dumps(payload), capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout). Exit codes come from scheduler/src/main.cpp: 0 OK, 1 error JSON, 2 wrong command-line flags.
6 Example
Hospital request committed → child started → reads 1.4 KB JSON → writes the plan → exits 0 → parent parses it.
7 Analogy
A manager (parent) hands a sealed envelope to a specialist (child), waits at the door, receives the answer and a thumbs-up or thumbs-down (exit code). If the specialist takes more than 10 seconds, the manager sends them home (kill).
9 Pros / limits
+ crash isolation, language independence, easy to test by hand. − start-up cost per call; JSON encoding cost.
10 Viva
Q: Did you use fork()? A: Not directly. Python's subprocess library makes the system calls (fork/exec or posix_spawn, pipe, wait). Our design decision was to run the scheduler as a child process connected by pipes. Follow-up: What is a zombie? A finished child whose exit status hasn't been collected; subprocess.run always collects it.

Process states and the PCB (as an analogy in our data) Theoretical analogy in data

We don't build a real PCB (Process Control Block, the kernel's record of a process). But our Request struct plays the same role for a water request, and request statuses look like process states:

PCB field (OS)Our request field
PIDrequest_id
Prioritypriority (from the organisation), urgency
Arrival / accounting infoarrival_time, deadline, wait_time, start_time, finish_time
Burst time (CPU needed)requested_litres ÷ flow rate
Statestatus in water_requests
   OS:      new -> ready -> running -> terminated            (+ waiting for I/O)
   Ours:   (POST /me/requests)
            pending ──(admin applies a plan)──> approved | partial | rejected      (final)
               └──(user cancels)──> cancelled                                     (final)
   "running" exists only inside the simulation (start_time .. finish_time).

Context switching Partial: simulated

Definition: saving one process's CPU state and loading another's. Ours: Round Robin moves to the next request after each 2,000 L turn. That is the simulated equivalent of a context switch. We do not model a switching cost (in real valves this would be the time to switch a supply line). Real context switches between our real processes (Uvicorn threads, scheduler children, PostgreSQL) are done by the Linux kernel. Indirect

Foreground and background execution Indirect

The ML pipeline is a batch job started by Compose that runs once and exits (restart: "no"). docker compose up -d runs containers in the background (detached). v2.0 adds a long-running background process: the backup loop (section J). Inside the API, all work is done in the foreground of each request; there are no background job queues. Not implemented (retention runs at start-up or on demand, not on a timer).

B. Threads and concurrency

Process vs thread, and multithreading Indirect (in the app) · Explicit (in tests)

1 Definition
A thread is a path of execution inside a process. Threads share the process's memory; processes don't share memory.
2 Why
A web server must serve several users at once. While one request waits for the database, another can run.
3 Internals
Linux schedules threads like processes (both are "tasks"). In CPython, the GIL allows one thread to run Python code at a time, but it is released during I/O (socket reads, waiting for a child process).
4 Ours
FastAPI runs every def endpoint in a thread pool (Starlette/AnyIO). Ours are all def, so two admins committing at once are two threads, each with its own DB connection. The tests create threads explicitly: threading.Thread ×4 with a threading.Barrier(4) to start them at the same instant.
5 Where
backend/tests/test_postgres.py: test_concurrent_commits_allocate_the_water_exactly_once; tests/concurrency_demo.py.
6 Example
4 threads → barrier releases all → each calls commit_allocation → see "Race condition" below.
7 Analogy
A process is a kitchen; threads are cooks in the same kitchen sharing the fridge. Separate processes are separate kitchens.
9 Pros / limits
+ overlap waiting time. − shared data needs locks; the GIL limits CPU-bound Python (our CPU-heavy part is in C++ anyway).
10 Viva
Q: Concurrency vs parallelism? A: Concurrency means dealing with many tasks over the same period (interleaving). Parallelism means executing at literally the same moment on different cores. Our API is concurrent (thread pool); PostgreSQL can run queries in parallel on several cores.

Race condition, critical section, mutual exclusion Explicit (handled via DB locks and a mutex)

1 Definition
A race condition is when the result depends on the timing of concurrent operations. A critical section is code that touches shared data and must not be run by two at once. Mutual exclusion guarantees only one is inside at a time.
2 Why
The reservoir's water level and the pending-request list are shared by all admins.
3 Internals
SELECT … FOR UPDATE takes an exclusive row lock held until COMMIT/ROLLBACK. A second transaction asking for the same lock blocks (sleeps) until it is free. A Python threading.Lock is a mutex built on an OS futex.
4–5 Ours
service.commit_allocation() (reservoir lock, then FOR UPDATE OF r on requests); auth.login() (account row, protecting the failure counter); portal.create_request() (organisation row, protecting "max 5 pending"); portal.cancel_request(); update_reservoir(); reset_demo(); admin_service approve/update; db._schema_lock (Python mutex). v1.0 had 10 FOR UPDATE statements and 2 advisory locks; v2.0 has 25 and 4 (policy approval, timetable publish, sensor readings, 2FA challenges, privacy requests…: see section J).
6 Example
See the timeline below. These are real results from concurrency_demo.py, re-run on 18 Oct 2026 on the v2.0 code (same result as on 12 Oct).
7 Analogy
One key to a shared locker: whoever has the key opens it; others queue at the door.
9 Pros / limits
+ correctness is guaranteed by the DBMS. − waiting reduces throughput; long critical sections hurt.
10 Viva
Q: Where exactly is your critical section? A: From SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the reservoir row to COMMIT in commit_allocation(). Follow-up: Why not just a Python lock? Because there could be several backend processes (or machines); the database is the one place all of them share.

T1: plan 80,000 L, write, COMMIT                     T1: plan, write, COMMIT -> lock released
T2: plan 80,000 L, write, COMMIT   <-- double!       T2: wakes, reads 0 pending -> 409 Conflict

Mutexes and semaphores

MechanismStatusDetail
Mutex (binary lock)Explicitthreading.Lock() in db.py and in security.RateLimiter (v2.0); DB row locks behave as per-row mutexes; pg_advisory_xact_lock(724001…724004) are named, database-wide mutexes across processes.
Counting semaphoreNot implementedClosest ideas: "at most 5 pending requests per organisation" and the rate limit (20 sign-in requests per minute) are limits enforced by counting under a lock, not a semaphore primitive.
BarrierExplicit (tests only)threading.Barrier(4) releases 4 threads together to provoke the race.

Deadlock, starvation, livelock

ConceptStatusExplanation
StarvationExplicit (prevented in Water-aware, measured for all)A request that never gets water. Measured as unserved_count. FCFS left 4 of 8 with 0 L in the sample; Priority 3; Water-aware 0 (guarantee floor). Also see the H section on deadlock.
DeadlockPartial (prevention by lock order + DBMS detection)Detailed in section H.
LivelockTheoreticalProcesses keep reacting to each other without progress. We have no retry loops between competing transactions, so it can't happen in our code.

Producer–consumer problem Theoretical analogy

Organisations produce requests (INSERT … status 'pending'); the admin's commit consumes all pending requests. The shared "buffer" is the set of pending rows in water_requests. The per-organisation limit of 5 is like a bounded buffer for each producer. Synchronisation comes from transactions and row locks, not from semaphores. A real producer–consumer implementation (e.g. a job queue with worker threads) is not implemented.

C. CPU scheduling: what we explicitly implemented

All four algorithms are Explicit implementations of scheduling policies, applied to water requests on a simulated pipeline. They don't schedule real CPU processes; Linux does that for our programs.

FCFS (First Come First Served) Explicit

1 Definition
Serve requests in order of arrival; non-preemptive.
2 Why
The baseline: it's how things are often done by default.
3 Internals
Picker: the minimum arrival_time; ties broken by the lowest request_id.
4–5 Ours
scheduler/src/fcfs.cpp, class Fcfs.
6 Example
Gantt above: the factory that arrived first takes 20,000 L, and the hospital finishes at minute 114 although it needed water by minute 60.
7 Analogy
A railway ticket queue.
9 Pros / limits
+ simple, predictable, no starvation in the CPU sense. − the convoy effect (big jobs hold up small ones); ignores importance; with limited water, later arrivals starve.
10 Viva
Q: Does FCFS cause starvation? A: For a CPU, no: everyone eventually runs. For water, yes, because the resource is consumed: when it runs out, the rest get nothing (4 of 8 in our sample).

Priority scheduling (non-preemptive) Explicit

1 Definition
Serve the highest-priority ready request; once started, it isn't interrupted.
3 Internals
Picker: highest priority, then earlier arrival, then lower id.
4–5 Ours
priority.cpp, class PriorityScheduler. The comment in the file states its weaknesses on purpose.
6 Example
Hospital first (20 min), then the priority-4 users; the park (priority 1) gets nothing.
7 Analogy
Hospital emergency triage.
8 Preemptive vs non-preemptive
Preemptive: a newly arrived higher-priority job interrupts the running one. Non-preemptive: it waits. We implement non-preemptive only. Preemptive priority is not implemented. With batch window "all", everything has already arrived anyway, so preemption would change little in the backend's default mode.
9 Pros / limits
+ important users first (best importance-weighted delivery under severe scarcity: 0.64–0.68 in experiments). − starvation of low priority; ignores urgency and size.
10 Viva
Q: How do OSes fix priority starvation? A: Aging: raise the priority of long-waiting processes. Our Water-aware rule uses a fairness factor, deadline pressure and the guarantee floor for the same purpose.

Round Robin Explicit

1 Definition
Each ready job gets a fixed time quantum, then goes to the back of the queue; preemptive by time.
3 Internals
A std::deque queue. Each turn grants min(quantum, still needed, water left), advances the clock, admits new arrivals, and re-queues the request if it's unfinished. New arrivals join before the request that was just served rejoins.
4–5 Ours
round_robin.cpp, class RoundRobin; quantum = quantum_litres = 2,000 L (= 4 minutes at 500 L/min). min_allocation_ratio is not applied, because water already delivered can't be taken back.
6 Example
Gantt above; Jain fairness 0.91, the highest.
7 Analogy
Passing one microphone around a group: everyone speaks for 30 seconds per turn.
9 Pros / limits
+ fair, shortest response times, no starvation. − ignores importance; many partial grants; quantum choice matters (too small = many switches; too large = FCFS). We reject absurdly small quanta (test_round_robin_rejects_absurd_quantum).
10 Viva
Q: What happens if the quantum is very large? A: RR becomes FCFS, since each request finishes in its first turn.

Water-aware (our own) Explicit

Covered in Phase 3, code section 2. In OS terms it is a dynamic, multi-factor priority scheduler with an anti-starvation reservation:

  • The dynamic part: deadline pressure grows as the clock advances, and scarcity changes as water is used.
  • Its "reservation" (the floor) has no direct textbook equivalent. It is closest to proportional-share ideas (each user is guaranteed a minimum share).

Measured across 600 scenarios: 0 requests left with nothing at moderate and severe scarcity. Not the fastest; not the fairest; best importance-weighted delivery only at moderate scarcity.

SJF (Shortest Job First) Not implemented

SJF picks the smallest burst (smallest litres) first. It minimises average waiting time, but can starve big jobs. It's easy to add: a new picker choosing the minimum requested_litres, about 20 lines like fcfs.cpp. If an examiner asks, say so honestly. You can also point out that Water-aware's scarcity factor favours smaller requests when water is scarce, a partial SJF-like effect.

D. Memory management

Main vs virtual memoryTheoreticalAll our processes use virtual memory provided by Linux. We don't configure or implement it.

The process also exits after each run, so the OS reclaims everything. Not measured with Valgrind. Not verified
Container memory limitsNot configuredCompose sets no mem_limit; cgroups could cap memory.

Q: "Where is memory management in your project?" A: "We didn't implement memory management. In our C++ we avoided leaks with RAII: smart pointers and STL containers instead of manual new/delete. Each scheduler run is a short process, so the OS reclaims all its memory when it exits. Paging and virtual memory are done by Linux underneath."

E. File and I/O management

ConceptStatusIn our project
File descriptorsIndirectThe scheduler uses fd 0 (stdin), fd 1 (stdout) and fd 2 (stderr), connected to pipes by the parent. Sockets (HTTP, PostgreSQL) are also file descriptors.
File operationsIndirectmigrations.apply() reads db/migrate.sql (Path.read_text). The ML pipeline writes results/metrics.json and PNG files. PostgreSQL writes data files and its WAL.
BufferingIndirectstd::cout is buffered and flushed at exit. Python reads all of stdout after the child finishes (capture_output). The print(..., flush=True) in db.py forces log lines out immediately so they show up in docker compose logs.
I/O handlingIndirectThe whole input is read in one go: std::string text((std::istreambuf_iterator<char>(std::cin)), …).

Resource managementExplicitConnections always closed (try/finally in get_conn); cursors and transactions closed with with; the 10 s timeout frees a stuck child; Docker volume pgdata for persistent storage.

F. System calls

1 Definition
A system call is how a program in user mode asks the kernel (running in kernel mode, with full hardware access) to do something privileged: create a process, read a file, open a network connection.
2 Library vs system call
subprocess.run(), std::cout and open() in Python are library functions. Inside them, the C library makes the actual system calls (write, read, pipe2, clone/fork, execve, wait4, socket, connect…).
3 Ours
Indirect. Our code never calls fork(), exec(), wait(), read() or write() by name. They happen underneath these operations:

Path.read_text()openat, read, close

H. Deadlock management

1 Definition
A set of processes, each waiting for a resource held by another in the set, so none can proceed.
2 Four necessary conditions (Coffman)
  1. Mutual exclusion: row locks are exclusive.
  2. Hold and wait: a transaction holds the reservoir lock while waiting for request locks.
  3. No preemption: a lock can't be taken away.
  4. Circular wait: T1 waits for T2, which waits for T1.
All four must hold at once for deadlock.
3 Prevention (ours)
Partial. We break circular wait with a consistent lock order: every allocation transaction locks the reservoir row first, then the request rows (ORDER BY arrival_time, request_id). Two commits can never hold locks in opposite orders. A second commit simply waits at the reservoir lock.
4 Avoidance
Not implemented. The Banker's algorithm (grant only if the system stays in a "safe state") isn't used. It needs advance knowledge of maximum needs, which is impractical for a database.
5 Detection and recovery
Indirect. PostgreSQL runs a deadlock detector after deadlock_timeout (default 1 s): it builds a wait-for graph, finds a cycle, and aborts one transaction (error 40P01). Our code would then roll back and return HTTP 500 (no automatic retry).
5b v2.0 lock orders
Sensor reading: device row → reservoir row. Commit: reservoir row → request rows. Policy approval: pending policy → active policy. Timetable publish: draft row → (update of the published row). No transaction takes two of these groups in opposite orders, so no new cycle appears. Reasoned, not tested for deadlock
6 Where a deadlock could appear
A user cancelling request #5 (locks request #5) while an admin commit (holding the reservoir lock) tries to lock request #5. The commit just waits for the cancel to finish. The cancel never asks for the reservoir lock, so there is no cycle. Reasoned, not tested
7 Analogy
Two cars at a narrow bridge each waiting for the other. A rule like "always enter from the north first" removes the circle.
10 Viva
Q: Which Coffman condition do you break? A: Circular wait, by ordering locks: reservoir, then requests. Follow-up: What if a deadlock happens anyway? PostgreSQL detects it, aborts one transaction; we roll back cleanly; the user can retry.
  Deadlock (avoided):                    Our order (no cycle possible):
  T1 holds A, waits B                    T1: lock reservoir -> lock requests -> ... COMMIT
  T2 holds B, waits A   (cycle)          T2: lock reservoir (WAIT until T1 commits) -> ...

J. OS concepts added or strengthened in v2.0 v2.0

Slot scheduling of a shared device: the zone timetable Explicit

1 Definition
Reservation-based scheduling gives each job fixed time slots on a shared resource in advance (as in time-division multiplexing or real-time systems that reserve CPU time per period). Packing jobs into slots with limited capacity is a form of bin packing.
2 Why needed
A pumping station can push only so many litres per hour, and each zone's main can take only so much. Zones must be given hours so the pump is never overloaded.
3 Internals (ours)
The day (05:00–23:00) is cut into 18 one-hour slots; free[t] is the pump capacity left in slot t. Zones are taken in priority order (like a priority scheduler admitting jobs), each gets the earliest continuous run of slots that can still carry its inlet rate (first-fit), otherwise its litres are split over whatever capacity is left.
4–5 Where
scheduler/src/timetable.cpp: build_timetable(), step 2.
6 Example
Normal day: North 05–11, Central 11–18, South 17–23 (South shares 17–18 with the end of Central: 377,777 + 450,000 L ≤ 1,000,000 L).
7 Analogy
Booking a single lab projector: the most important class books first and takes the earliest free block that fits the whole lecture.
9 Pros / limits
+ simple, predictable, never overloads. − greedy first-fit is not optimal; high-priority zones always get the earliest hours.
10 Viva
Q: Is the timetable preemptive? A: No. Once a block is placed it isn't moved for a later zone; it is non-preemptive, offline (all zones known in advance) scheduling.

Proportional share with guarantees: floors + water-filling Explicit

1 Definition
Proportional-share scheduling gives each consumer a share of a resource in proportion to a weight (lottery and stride scheduling, Linux CFS weights). A guaranteed minimum (reservation) is honoured first, as with cgroup minimums for CPU or memory.
2 In our project
Two places: (a) Water-aware keeps each waiting request's class share in reserve (pending_floor_litres); (b) the timetable first gives every zone its floor (30% of its target in policy v1), then shares the rest by weight = priority × (1 − floor) × target, capping zones that are full and re-sharing their excess (water-filling).
3 Why it matters for OS
The same trade-off as CPU schedulers: pure priority starves, pure equality ignores importance. Weights + minimums are how real kernels and hypervisors balance the two.
10 Viva
Q: What is water-filling? A: Pour the budget into all unfilled zones in proportion to their weights; when a zone is full, stop pouring into it and share what's left among the others; repeat.

Count in v2.0: 25 FOR UPDATE statements in the backend (admin_service 2, auth 3, mfa 3, network 2, policy 4, portal 2, privacy 2, service 5, telemetry 2), 4 advisory locks (724001 upgrade, 724002 bootstrap, 724003 demo approver, 724004 app role) and 2 Python mutexes (db._schema_lock, RateLimiter._lock). Code

Time and clocks Indirect / Explicit use

  • Wall-clock time (time.time()) drives TOTP: server and phone must agree on the time to within about ±30 s (the window accepts the previous and next code). Real servers keep their clocks right with NTP, which the OS does. Indirect
  • Monotonic time (time.monotonic()) drives the rate limiter, because it never jumps backwards if someone changes the system clock. Explicit choice
  • Expiry as a timeout: sessions (12 h), sign-in challenges (5 min), "sensor offline" after 30 min, lockout 5 min. All computed in SQL with now().

Long-running background process and supervision Config

The backup container is a daemon-like process: an infinite loop that works, then sleeps 24 hours. Compose's restart: unless-stopped acts as a process supervisor (like systemd or init): if the API, database, web server or backup process dies, Docker starts it again. The ML job is still a one-shot batch process (restart: "no"). Restart behaviour not tested here

Admission control and idempotency Explicit

  • Rate limiting is admission control: refuse work early (429) rather than let one client overload the system.
  • Idempotent ingestion: UNIQUE (device_id, measured_at) + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING means a gateway may resend after a timeout ("at-least-once" delivery) without double counting, a classic distributed-systems technique.

v2.0 mein OS ke teen naye "explicit" kaam: (1) timetable = shared pump pe time-slot booking, (2) floors + water-filling = proportional share with guarantee, (3) rate limiter ka threading.Lock = humare apne Python code mein mutex. Baaki sab (clock, NTP, Docker restart) OS/Docker karta hai: woh "indirect" bolna.

Phase 4 wrap-up

Summary. What we implemented:

  • scheduling policies, metrics and starvation prevention (as a water simulation);
  • mutual exclusion through DB row locks, a mutex and advisory locks;
  • deadlock prevention through lock ordering;
  • v2.0: slot scheduling of zones on a shared pump, proportional share with guaranteed minimums, a mutex-protected rate limiter.

What we use from the OS: process creation, pipes, exit codes, threads, system calls, isolation. What is only theoretical: paging, virtual memory, shared memory.

Remember:

  • the three-way distinction (explicit / indirect / theoretical);
  • Gantt charts of the 4 rules;
  • Coffman conditions and which one we break;
  • RR wait = response time;
  • SJF not implemented;
  • timetable = non-preemptive, offline slot scheduling;
  • 25 FOR UPDATE / 4 advisory locks / 2 mutexes;
  • RAII.
1. In Round Robin, is our wait_time the total waiting time?No. It's the time until the first turn (response time). Total waiting would also include the gaps between later turns.
2. Which Coffman condition does our design break, and how?Circular wait. All allocation transactions lock the reservoir row first, then the request rows in a fixed order, so no cycle of waits can form.
3. Name two system calls that happen when the backend runs the scheduler.Examples: pipe2 (create pipes), clone/execve or posix_spawn (start the child), write/read (send and receive JSON), wait4 (collect the exit status). They happen inside Python's subprocess, not in our code directly.
4. Why can FCFS starve requests in our project but not on a CPU?CPU time is renewable: every process eventually gets a turn. Water is consumed: once 50,000 L are given away, later requests get nothing.
4b. Why does the rate limiter need its own lock if PostgreSQL already has locks?Its counters live in Python memory, not in the database. FastAPI serves requests on several threads, so "count, compare, append" must be one atomic step: with self._lock: makes it a critical section.
5. Why use a separate process for the scheduler instead of a thread?Isolation (a crash can't take down the API), language independence (C++ vs Python), a simple, testable interface (pipes + JSON), and a timeout can kill it cleanly.

TermMeaningIn JalRakshak
Data / database / DBMS / RDBMSFacts / an organised collection / software managing it / a DBMS storing data as related tables"Hospital asked 10,000 L" / the jalrakshak database / PostgreSQL / PostgreSQL is an RDBMS
Schema vs instanceStructure (rarely changes) vs the data at one momentSchema = schema.sql + migrate.sql (24 tables in v2.0). Instance = today's rows (e.g. 8 users, 1 reservoir, 50,000 L, 1 approved policy).
Table, row, column, data typeRelation, tuple, attribute, domainwater_requests; one request; requested_litres; NUMERIC(12,2)
Types we use—SERIAL/BIGSERIAL (auto-numbered integer), INTEGER, SMALLINT, NUMERIC(12,2) (exact decimal; no floating-point error for litres), TEXT, BOOLEAN, DATE, TIMESTAMPTZ (timestamp with time zone), JSONB (binary JSON)
Primary key (PK)Column(s) that uniquely identify a row; never NULLEvery table: zone_id, request_id… sessions.token_hash is a natural (non-numeric) PK.
Foreign key (FK)A column referring to another table's PKwater_requests.user_id REFERENCES users(user_id)
Superkey / candidate keyAny set of columns that is unique / a minimal such setzones: candidate keys {zone_id} and {name} (UNIQUE). {zone_id, population} is a superkey but not minimal.
Composite keyA key made of 2+ columnsUNIQUE (run_id, request_id) on allocations; UNIQUE (zone_id, recorded_on) on consumption; UNIQUE (zone_id, target_date, model_name) on predictions
ConstraintsRules the DBMS enforcesNOT NULL, DEFAULT, CHECK (e.g. priority BETWEEN 1 AND 5, deadline > arrival_time, available_litres <= capacity_litres), UNIQUE, FK. One clever CHECK: CHECK (role = 'admin' OR status <> 'active' OR user_id IS NOT NULL), meaning "an active requester must belong to an organisation".
NULL"Unknown / not applicable", not zeroaccounts.user_id is NULL for admins; allocations.score is NULL except for Water-aware; locked_until NULL = not locked
Entity integrityThe PK is unique and not NULLGuaranteed by every PRIMARY KEY
Referential integrityEvery FK value exists in the parent tableInserting a request for user 999 fails with 23503 → our API returns 404 "user_id or reservoir_id does not exist"

B. Database design: the ER model

Entities, attributes and relationships

 ZONES (zone_id PK, name UQ, population)
   1 ──< USERS = organisations (user_id PK, name, user_type, priority 1..5, zone_id FK)
   1 ──< CONSUMPTION (consumption_id PK, zone_id FK, recorded_on, litres, is_injected_leak; UQ(zone_id,recorded_on))
   1 ──< PREDICTIONS (prediction_id PK, zone_id FK, target_date, predicted_litres, model_name; UQ(zone,date,model))
   1 ──< ALERTS      (alert_id PK, zone_id FK NULL, alert_type, severity, message, resolved)
   1 ──< ISSUES      (issue_id PK, ..., zone_id FK NULL)

 USERS 1 ──< WATER_REQUESTS (request_id PK, user_id FK, reservoir_id FK, requested_litres, urgency,
                              arrival_time, deadline, status, created_by FK->accounts NULL, note)

   1 ──< WATER_REQUESTS

                    wait_minutes, score, allocated_at; UQ(run_id, request_id))

   ..... linked to PREDICTIONS by model_name (logical join, NO foreign key)

Design decisions in the new tables

DecisionWhyTrade-off
Policy class values as JSONB maps ({"hospital": 5, …})A policy is a versioned document: it is proposed, compared and approved as a whole and never edited after approval. One row = one version.A 1NF relaxation. The normalised alternative is policy_classes(policy_id, class, priority, min_share). The database cannot CHECK each value, so policy.validate() does it (priorities 1–5, shares 0–1, weights ≥ 0).
Status columns + partial unique indexes"Exactly one approved policy" and "one published timetable per day" are rules about some rows only. A partial index enforces uniqueness only where its WHERE holds.PostgreSQL-specific syntax (not in every DBMS).
supply_timetables.input / result as JSONBA snapshot of exactly what was computed and published (like audit_log.actor). Later network changes must not rewrite history.Not queryable column by column; the zone rows inside are read in Python.
devices: one table, two kinds, a CHECK choosing the FKA generalisation (device → level sensor | flow meter) stored in one table: CHECK ((kind = 'reservoir_level' AND reservoir_id IS NOT NULL) OR (kind = 'zone_flow' AND zone_id IS NOT NULL)).Some NULL columns; the alternative is one table per subtype.
readings: BIGSERIAL and UNIQUE (device_id, measured_at)Many rows (a reading every few seconds); the composite key makes resends harmless.Would need partitioning by time at real scale.
tanker_trips.planned_for kept even when timetable_id is setManual orders have no timetable, so the date must be stored anyway.For timetable orders it is derivable from the timetable's date (a small transitive dependency, accepted).
Anonymise instead of DELETE on erasureDecisions and audit rows refer to the account; deleting it would break FKs and the department's records. Personal fields are overwritten and anonymised_at set.The account row remains, without personal data.

Cardinality and relationship types

RelationshipTypeHow it's implemented
Zone has organisations1 : NFK users.zone_id
Organisation makes requests1 : NFK water_requests.user_id
Source feeds zones v2.01 : NFK zones.reservoir_id
Policy used by runs / timetables v2.01 : NFK policy_id in both
Policy proposed by / decided by v2.0two 1 : N to accountsproposed_by, decided_by
Device sends readings v2.01 : N, existence-dependentFK with ON DELETE CASCADE
Run allocates to requestsM : NAssociative table allocations with two FKs and UNIQUE(run_id, request_id)
Organisation has sign-in accounts1 : N (an account has 0 or 1 organisation)Nullable FK accounts.user_id
Account has sessions / notifications1 : N, existence-dependentFK with ON DELETE CASCADE
Issue reported by / handled bytwo 1 : N relationships to the same tableissues.account_id, issues.handled_by
One-to-one—None in the strict sense. schema_info is a single-row table (CHECK (id = 1)).

Strong and weak entities

Strong entities have their own identity: zones, reservoirs, users, accounts. Weak-like entities depend on a parent for meaning:

  • allocations (meaningless without its run and request; naturally identified by (run_id, request_id));
  • sessions, notifications, login_challenges (deleted with their account: ON DELETE CASCADE);
  • readings (deleted with their device; naturally identified by (device_id, measured_at)).

We gave them surrogate PKs anyway (simpler joins). Strictly speaking that makes them strong entities in the schema, with the dependency enforced by FKs and UNIQUE.

Converting ER to tables (the rules we followed)

  1. Each entity becomes a table; its key becomes the PK.
  2. A 1:N relationship becomes an FK on the "N" side (e.g. water_requests.user_id).
  3. An M:N relationship becomes a new table holding both FKs (allocations), plus the relationship's own attributes (allocated_litres, wait_minutes, score).
  4. A multivalued attribute becomes a separate table (daily consumption per zone → consumption).

Normalisation (checked table by table)

Normal formRule (simple words)Our status
1NFAtomic values; no repeating groupsYes for all regular columns. Exception by design: scheduler_runs.metrics and audit_log.details are JSONB documents (v2.0 adds more: policy class maps, timetable input/result, run comparison and overrides, zone boundaries; see the design decisions above). They are read and written as a whole, never queried inside, so we treat each as one value. Strict theorists would call this a 1NF relaxation.
2NF1NF + no non-key column depends on part of a composite keyYes. All PKs are single surrogate columns, so partial dependency can't occur. The natural composite keys ((run_id, request_id)) have attributes depending on both parts.
3NF2NF + no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency)Mostly yes, with two deliberate exceptions:
  1. allocations.reservoir_id can be derived via request_id → water_requests.reservoir_id (transitive). It was kept to make "delete all allocations of reservoir 1" (reset_demo) a simple query.
  2. audit_log.actor copies the account's email at that moment. It's a historical snapshot, intentionally not updated.
BCNFEvery determinant is a candidate keyHolds for the core tables except the two exceptions above. Example check: in zones, name → population, and name is a candidate key (UNIQUE), so it's fine.

Q: "Isn't users.priority determined by user_type? That would be a transitive dependency." A: "In v2.0 the default comes from the active policy's class priority, copied when the policy is approved. But the admin can set an exception for one organisation (priority_override = TRUE), e.g. a particular school. So user_type alone doesn't determine priority: there's no FD and no 3NF violation. Storing the copy also keeps old decisions explainable after a policy changes."

Functional dependencies (examples)

  • request_id → user_id, reservoir_id, requested_litres, urgency, arrival_time, deadline, status
  • user_id → name, user_type, priority, zone_id
  • zone_id → name, population; also name → zone_id
  • (run_id, request_id) → allocated_litres, wait_minutes, score
  • lower(email) → account_id

Anomalies we avoid:

  • Update anomaly: a zone's population is stored once in zones, not copied into every request. Changing it is one UPDATE.
  • Insertion anomaly: you can create a zone with no organisations yet.
  • Deletion anomaly: deleting a request doesn't delete the organisation's data. And we refuse to delete a zone that still has organisations (delete_zone → 409).
