  • P4: the department's part (audit, hosting, SSO, data, pilot).

Scale only on measured need.

Remember:

  • each improvement must name the problem it solves;
  • "configured" is not "verified": HTTPS and backups still need a run;
  • the 5 scaling stages; v2.0 is ready for stage 2.
1. What is the single most important next step, and why?Run v2.0 with scripts\test.ps1 on your own laptop, and try the HTTPS profile and one backup/restore. Everything else is unverified in your real environment until then.
2. How would you shorten the time rows are locked during a commit?Compute the plan and the comparison without locks. Then, in a short transaction, lock the reservoir, check that nothing changed (e.g. a version number), and write. If something changed, recompute (optimistic concurrency control).
3. Why not use Kubernetes now?It solves multi-machine orchestration, which a single-city system doesn't need. Compose on one VM (with the HTTPS profile) is enough until load proves otherwise.
4. Which remaining security gap is cheapest to close?Encrypting the TOTP secrets with a key kept outside the database (a few lines with an encryption library), followed by turning on REQUIRE_ADMIN_MFA=1 in any shared deployment.
5. Which v1.0 roadmap items did v2.0 implement?Any five: editable policy (with approval), per-class floors, decision record export, Hindi for organisations, least-privilege DB user, TRUNCATE protection, backups, retention, rate limiting, two-factor sign-in, CSP, restart policies, meter data interface, multi-source timetable.

Phase 10 · Viva and presentation preparation

Format of each card: Q · Simple answer (say this first) · Deeper (if they push) · Code reference · Likely follow-up.

Level 1: Basic

1. What is JalRakshak?
Simple
A web app for a water department that decides how limited water is shared among organisations and (v2.0) which zone gets supply at which hours, using OS scheduling ideas, with every decision stored safely and accountably in a database.
Deeper
Requests are processes, the pipeline is the CPU. Four allocation rules are compared on the same data before one is applied in a locked transaction.
Reference
README.md, scheduler/, service.commit_allocation()
Follow-up
"Why call it scheduling and not just allocation?" Because order matters too (waiting time, deadlines), not only amounts.
2. What problem does it solve?
Simple
When demand is higher than supply (e.g. 80,000 L asked, 50,000 L available), deciding fairly and safely who gets what.
Deeper
Context: NITI Aayog's 2018 index reported about 600 million Indians under high to extreme water stress; Indian cities often supply water only a few hours a day (Phase 7 sources).
Reference
Phase 7
Follow-up
"Have you tested it with a real utility?" No; synthetic data only. v2.0 can take real meter data and has a shadow mode for a pilot, but none has been done. Say it clearly.
3. What are the objectives?
Simple
Implement and compare scheduling rules for water; prevent starvation; store decisions safely under concurrency; forecast demand and detect leaks; provide secure panels.
Deeper
Measured by wait time, Jain fairness, importance-weighted delivery, unserved count and missed deadlines.
Reference
compute_metrics()
Follow-up
"Which objective was hardest?" Concurrency safety, proved with the 4-thread test.
4. What are the main features?
Simple
  • A user panel: request water, track results, report problems, notifications.
  • An admin panel with 11 tabs: Overview, Allocate (compare, apply, override, shadow), Supply (timetable, map, tankers), Forecast, Records (decision records), Policy, Accounts, Issues, Field data, Compliance, Settings.
Deeper
95 API endpoints; 24 tables; 4 allocation rules + manual mode + zone timetable; 4 forecast models; 2 leak detectors; English/Hindi user panel.
Reference
main.py, AdminApp.jsx, UserApp.jsx
Follow-up
"Show me the audit log." (Demo it: Compliance › Audit log in v2.0.)
5. Which technologies did you use?
Simple
C++ for the scheduler, Python FastAPI for the backend, PostgreSQL for the database, React for the frontend, scikit-learn for ML, Docker to run everything.
Deeper
The backend runs the C++ as a child process connected by pipes; psycopg2 is the DB driver; nginx serves the frontend.
Reference
Phase 2 table
Follow-up
"Why C++ and Python both?" C++ for the OS-style core and speed; Python for the web and ML ecosystem.
6. What is FCFS / Round Robin / Priority scheduling?
Simple
FCFS: serve in arrival order. Priority: most important first. Round Robin: everyone gets a fixed slice in turn (here 2,000 L).
Deeper
Ours are non-preemptive except RR; burst = litres ÷ 500 L/min.
Reference
fcfs.cpp, priority.cpp, round_robin.cpp
Follow-up
"What is the convoy effect?" A big job at the front makes everyone wait (Metro Steel's 20,000 L in FCFS).
7. What is a primary key / foreign key?
Simple
A PK uniquely identifies a row; an FK points to a PK in another table.
Deeper
water_requests.user_id → users.user_id. An invalid id gives error 23503 → our API returns 404.
Reference
schema.sql
Follow-up
"Composite key example?" UNIQUE(run_id, request_id) in allocations.
8. Who are the users?
Simple
Organisation staff (requesters) and water-department administrators.
Deeper
Role column in accounts; sign-ups need admin approval.
Reference
auth.register, admin_service.approve
Follow-up
"Can a requester see other organisations?" No: filtered by their organisation, 404 otherwise.

Level 2: Intermediate

9. Explain the architecture.
Simple
Three tiers: React → FastAPI → PostgreSQL, plus a C++ scheduler called by the backend and an ML job that writes forecasts to the DB.
Deeper
Docker Compose runs 4 services; the backend waits for a healthy DB; the browser sends a Bearer token.
Reference
Phase 2 flow diagram
Follow-up
"Where is business logic?" service.py, portal.py, auth.py, admin_service.py; not in React.
10. How does the backend talk to the C++ program?
Simple
It starts it as a child process, writes JSON to its input and reads JSON from its output.
Deeper
subprocess.run([binary], input=…, capture_output=True, timeout=10): pipes, exit code 0/1, kill on timeout.
Reference
scheduler_client.run_scheduler
Follow-up
"Why not a library call?" Isolation, language independence, testability.
11. Explain the Water-aware algorithm.
Simple
It gives each waiting request a score from 5 factors and serves the highest first, but caps each grant so that everyone still waiting keeps 30% of their request in reserve.
Deeper
  • Weights: priority 0.30, urgency 0.25, scarcity 0.15, population 0.15, fairness 0.15.
  • Urgency includes deadline pressure.
  • Cap = max(0.3 × asked, left − 0.3 × others' asks).
Reference
water_aware.cpp
Follow-up
"Why 0.3?" A policy choice. In experiments 0.2 was the smallest value that left nobody empty; 0.3 was kept as a balance and not tuned further.
12. Explain your database schema.
Simple
24 tables: zones, organisations, reservoirs, requests, runs and allocations for decisions; consumption, predictions, model scores and alerts for ML; accounts, sessions, notifications, issues and audit log for the panels; and in v2.0 policies, supply timetables, tanker trips, devices, readings, sign-in challenges, privacy requests and security incidents.
Deeper
allocations resolves the M:N relationship between runs and requests. Mostly 3NF, with 2 deliberate exceptions.
Reference
Phase 5 ER diagram
Follow-up
"Name a CHECK constraint." CHECK (available_litres >= 0) and <= capacity_litres.
13. Walk through one SQL query.
Simple
The pending-requests query joins requests, organisations and zones, filters status 'pending' for the reservoir, sorts by arrival, and during commit locks the request rows.
Deeper
EXPLAIN shows a bitmap index scan on idx_requests_status and PK index lookups.
Reference
service.PENDING_SQL
Follow-up
"What does FOR UPDATE OF r mean?" Lock only rows from the alias r (water_requests).
14. What happens when the admin clicks Apply?
Simple
One transaction locks the reservoir and pending requests, runs the chosen rule, saves the plan, reduces the water level, notifies organisations, writes an audit row, and commits.
Deeper
Any error → rollback; a second simultaneous click gets 409.
Reference
commit_allocation()
Follow-up
"Why notifications in the same transaction?" So you can never have a plan without notices, or notices for a plan that rolled back.
15. How does sign-in work?
Simple
The password is checked against a salted PBKDF2 hash; on success the server creates a random token and stores only its SHA-256 hash; the browser sends the token on each request.
Deeper
Lockout after 5 failures; same error for unknown email; 12 h expiry; forced password change for the first admin.
Reference
auth.py
Follow-up
"Why hash the token?" A database leak shouldn't give working sessions.
16. How is the ML connected to scheduling?
Simple
The ML job writes today's demand forecast; Water-aware uses it in the scarcity factor.
Deeper
FORECAST_TODAY_SQL sums predictions of the selected model. If there is none, it falls back to the litres still requested.
Reference
service._forecast_today, _plan
Follow-up
"Which model and how accurate?" Random forest, MAE 1,223 L (5.1%) on 90 held-out synthetic days.
17. Why PostgreSQL and not MongoDB?
Simple
We need transactions, row locks, joins and constraints. That's relational strength.
Deeper
The core safety guarantee (no double allocation) depends on FOR UPDATE and CHECK constraints.
Reference
Phase 5 D
Follow-up
"And MySQL?" It would also work (InnoDB has row locks); we chose PostgreSQL for its CHECK constraints, JSONB, advisory locks and transactional DDL.
18. Which design pattern(s) did you use?
Simple
Strategy (pickers), factory (make_scheduler), dependency injection (FastAPI Depends), layered architecture.
Deeper
Polymorphic Scheduler::run; RAII in C++.
Reference
scheduler.cpp, main.py
Follow-up
"Benefit of the strategy pattern here?" A fair comparison: one engine, only the choice differs.

Level 3: Advanced

19. Prove that two admins can't allocate the same water twice.
Simple
The reservoir row is locked first, so the second transaction waits; when it continues, nothing is pending, so it gets 409.
Deeper
Test: 4 threads with a barrier → 1 commit, 3 conflicts; used + left = 50,000. Removing the locks → 2 runs and 160,000 L allocated.
Reference
test_postgres.py, concurrency_demo.py
Follow-up
"Isn't the CHECK constraint enough?" No: with 200,000 L available, both plans fit, so the CHECK never fires; only the lock prevents it.
20. What isolation level do you use, and is it enough?
Simple
PostgreSQL's default, READ COMMITTED, and yes, because we lock the rows we change.
Deeper
After waiting for a lock, READ COMMITTED re-checks the row, so the second commit sees the requests are no longer pending. Phantoms (new requests) are harmless here.
Reference
Phase 5 D
Follow-up
"What would SERIALIZABLE change?" A conflicting transaction would abort with error 40001 and need a retry loop.
21. Can a deadlock occur?
Simple
We prevent the common cause by always locking in the same order: reservoir, then requests. If one happens anyway, PostgreSQL detects it and aborts one transaction.
Deeper
That breaks the circular-wait condition. Detection runs after deadlock_timeout (1 s); error 40P01 → rollback → HTTP 500.
Reference
commit_allocation()
Follow-up
"Do you retry?" No; that's a possible improvement.
22. How do you avoid floating-point errors in litres?
Simple
The C++ rounds every grant down to 0.01 L; Python sums with Decimal; the DB stores NUMERIC(12,2).
Deeper
Rounding down guarantees the total never exceeds the available water. check_invariants verifies it after rounding.
Reference
round_down_to_cents, commit_allocation
Follow-up
"Better approach?" Integer centilitres everywhere.
23. What is the time complexity of your schedulers?
Simple
About O(n²) for FCFS, Priority and Water-aware (each step scans the ready list); Round Robin is about O(total litres ÷ quantum + n).
Deeper
Measured: 5,000 requests take ~0.2–0.3 s; 8 requests ~3 ms (including process start).
Reference
Phase 8 performance table
Follow-up
"How to make it O(n log n)?" A heap; Water-aware needs care because scores change over time.
24. What happens if the database goes down?
Simple
The API retries the connection 5 times, then returns 503 with a clear message; nothing half-written is left, because transactions are atomic.
Deeper
An OperationalError mid-request → 503 "database connection lost". Durability comes from the WAL. v2.0 adds daily pg_dump backups (14 days) and restore scripts (configured, not yet run here).
Reference
db.connect, main.py handlers
Follow-up
"Tested?" The 503 path isn't covered by an automated test. Be honest.
25. How do you prevent SQL injection?
Simple
All values are passed as parameters (%s), never concatenated into SQL.
Deeper
The few f-strings in SQL only insert fixed column or table names chosen by our code.
Reference
every cur.execute(sql, params)
Follow-up
"What about the scheduler?" It gets JSON via stdin and no shell (subprocess.run([binary])), so there's no shell injection either.
26. How do you evaluate the forecast honestly?
Simple
Train on older data and test on the last 90 days, never on random days. We compare against simple baselines.
Deeper
Leak days are cleaned before training. Random forest MAE 1,223 L vs seasonal-naive 1,849 L.
Reference
forecast.evaluate_models, ml/results/metrics.json
Follow-up
"Isn't 5% error suspiciously good?" The data is synthetic and smoother than reality; real data would be harder.
27. Why is the audit log trustworthy?
Simple
Rows are written in the same transaction as the change, and a database trigger refuses any update or delete.
Deeper
v2.0 closed the v1.0 gaps: a statement-level trigger blocks TRUNCATE, and the app's login has UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE on the audit log revoked. The table owner could still drop triggers; shipping rows to write-once storage would be the next step.
Reference
migrate.sql, audit.write
Follow-up
"Show it." Run DELETE FROM audit_log; in psql and show the exception.
28. What are alternative designs you considered?
Simple
Writing the scheduler in Python; using an ORM; using SERIALIZABLE instead of row locks; a microservice for the scheduler.
Deeper
We chose C++ as a child process for isolation and the OS connection; raw SQL for visible DBMS concepts; row locks for simple, explainable safety.
Reference
Phases 2–3
Follow-up
"Downside of your choice?" Process start-up per call; locks held while computing.

Level 4: Critical examiner

29. Why did you choose this technology stack?
Simple
Each piece maps to a need: C++ for the OS-style algorithms, PostgreSQL for transactions and locks, FastAPI for a quick, typed API, React for two rich panels, Docker so it runs on any laptop.
Deeper
Alternatives were considered (Phase 2, column 10).
Follow-up
"Isn't C++ overkill?" At 8 requests, yes for speed. It's there for the OS-subject alignment, determinism and process isolation.
30. Which OS concepts did YOU implement?
Simple
The scheduling policies (FCFS, non-preemptive Priority, Round Robin, our Water-aware rule), their metrics and starvation prevention, as a simulation of water delivery. We also designed the use of processes, pipes, locks and lock ordering.
Deeper
We did not implement paging, virtual memory, real CPU scheduling or system calls. The OS does those.
Follow-up
"So is this really an OS project?" It applies OS scheduling and synchronisation theory to a new resource, and uses real OS mechanisms (processes, pipes, threads) in the system.
31. Which features rely on the OS or DBMS automatically?
Simple
OS: process creation, pipes, thread switching, memory, isolation. DBMS: lock manager, MVCC, deadlock detection, durability, query planning.
Deeper
Our part is to use them correctly: where to lock, transaction boundaries, timeouts.
Follow-up
"Give one place you'd break things by misusing them." Locking requests before the reservoir in a different code path could create a deadlock cycle.
32. How do you prove a feature actually works?
Simple
Automated tests: 10,425 C++ checks, 77 backend tests against a real PostgreSQL, 11 ML tests, plus a reproducible concurrency demo and a browser walkthrough of the v2.0 screens.
Deeper
Hand-calculated numbers for the sample; fuzz tests for invariants; with/without-lock comparison.
Follow-up
"Did you run them on your machine?" Answer truthfully. Ideally run scripts\test.ps1 before the viva.
33. What is the weakest part of the project?
Simple
The data is synthetic, and the Water-aware weights are judgement calls, not validated with a water authority.
Deeper
Also technical: no connection pool; the Allocate tab still uses reservoir 1; the scheduler (up to 5 runs in v2.0) runs while rows are locked; 2FA secrets unencrypted; HTTPS and backups configured but not yet run.
Follow-up
"How would you validate the weights?" Workshops with a utility; sensitivity analysis; pilot comparison.
34. What would you change if you rebuilt it?
Simple
Integer litres end to end, a connection pool, versioned migrations, routers instead of one 95-route main.py, and computing the plan and comparison before locking (optimistic check). (Policy settings, from v1.0's list, are now done.)
Deeper
Possibly the scheduler as a library (pybind11) to avoid process start-up, keeping the CLI for tests.
Follow-up
"Why didn't you do that now?" Time, and the child-process design demonstrates OS concepts clearly.
35. What is technically novel, if anything?
Simple
The Water-aware rule's guarantee floor: a cap that reserves a minimum share for everyone still waiting. It's a simple, tunable way to trade importance for fairness on a consumable resource. We also measured that trade-off.
Deeper
Honestly, it's an engineering combination of known ideas (weighted priority, aging, proportional share), not a research breakthrough. We haven't done a literature survey to claim originality.
Follow-up
"Show the trade-off." The floor table in experiments/README.md (0 → 0.5: fairness up, importance-weighted delivery down).
36. Why didn't you implement SJF?
Simple
We chose rules that matched water policy questions (order, importance, fairness). SJF is easy to add: a new picker of about 20 lines.
Deeper
Water-aware's scarcity factor partly favours small requests when water is short.
Follow-up
"What's SJF's risk?" Starvation of large requests.
37. Is the time model realistic?
Simple
For organisation requests it's simplified: one pipeline at a fixed 500 L/min, serving one request at a time. The v2.0 zone timetable is closer to practice: zones are supplied in parallel within pump and inlet capacities per hour.
Deeper
Still no pressures, valves or looped pipes: a hydraulic model (EPANET) would be needed.
Follow-up
"Then why simulate time at all?" To measure waiting and deadlines, the OS analogy's core metrics.
38. How do you justify academic relevance?
Simple
It applies OS scheduling and synchronisation theory and DBMS transaction theory to a real resource-allocation problem, with measurable evidence for each claim.
Deeper
Concepts covered with code: scheduling, starvation, aging-like fairness, IPC, critical sections, deadlock prevention; keys, normalisation, ACID, isolation, locking, triggers, indexes.
Follow-up
"Which single experiment best shows both subjects?" The concurrency demo: OS threads + DB locks.
39. What happens if many users submit requests at once?
Simple
Each submission is its own short transaction; users of the same organisation are serialised by a row lock (to enforce max 5 pending); different organisations don't block each other.
Deeper
The bottleneck at large scale would be connections (no pool) and the thread-pool size. The rate limiter (600 API requests a minute per address) also protects the server.
Follow-up
"Load-tested?" No. Planned with locust or k6.
40. Your forecast uses synthetic data. Isn't it meaningless?
Simple
It shows the method works end to end: model comparison, time-based evaluation, and feeding the scheduler. The accuracy numbers don't predict real-world accuracy.
Deeper
The generator includes season, weekday, trend, heat waves, noise and injected leaks, so detectors and models are tested against known ground truth.
Follow-up
"What would change with real data?" Lower accuracy, missing values, meter errors; more cleaning.

Level 5: v2.0 (water-authority requirements) v2.0

41. What changed in version 2.0, and why?
Simple
We reviewed the project as a water department would before a pilot, and added what it asked for: an approved water policy with maker-checker, officer overrides with reasons and decision records, a zone-wise supply timetable with tankers, sensor and meter data, and security and privacy (2FA, HTTPS, least privilege, backups, DPDP).
Deeper
docs/compliance.md maps every requirement to the code and the test that proves it, and lists what only the department can do (audit, hosting, SSO).
Reference
CHANGES.md v2.0, docs/compliance.md
Follow-up
"Did a real department ask for this?" No. We wrote the review ourselves from a department's point of view. Say so.
42. What is maker-checker, and how is it enforced?
Simple
One officer proposes a policy change, a different officer approves it. The server refuses self-approval with 403.
Deeper
Enforced in policy.decide() by comparing proposed_by with the approver's account id, inside a transaction that locks the pending and the active policy. The partial unique index guarantees only one active policy.
Reference
policy.decide(), policies_one_active; test test_policy_needs_a_second_officer_and_sets_class_priorities
Follow-up
"What if there's only one admin?" REQUIRE_SECOND_APPROVER=0; self-approval is then marked in the audit log.
43. How does the policy change the scheduling?
Simple
The active policy gives each class a priority and a guaranteed share; Water-aware keeps every waiting request's share in reserve.
Deeper
Cap = max(own share × asked, water left − Σ others' share × asked). Policy v1 gives everyone 0.3, so the v1.0 results are unchanged; raising the park's share to 0.9 guaranteed it 3,600 of its 4,000 L in the test.
Reference
water_aware.cpp, floor_share_of(), policy.scheduler_settings()
Follow-up
"Can the weights change?" Yes, they're in the policy too, so a weight change also needs approval.
44. How do you stop an officer's override from being abused?
Simple
It needs a reason (at least 10 characters), can't exceed what was asked or what's available, and is recorded with the plan-vs-final litres, the policy and the comparison of all rules.
Deeper
The edited plan is re-run through the scheduler's manual mode, so its metrics are comparable. The organisation is told "set by the officer". The override rate is a pilot indicator.
Reference
service._apply_overrides(), manual.cpp, report.py
Follow-up
"Should big overrides need approval?" A good next step: maker-checker above a threshold.
45. Explain the supply timetable algorithm.
Simple
First decide how much each zone gets: everyone gets a guaranteed share of its target, the rest is shared by priority and need. Then decide when: the most important zone takes the earliest continuous block of hours the pump can still carry.
Deeper
Target = min(population × 135, inlet × hours). Weighted water-filling with weight = priority × (1 − share) × target. Slot placement is greedy first-fit over hourly pump capacity. Invariants: release, pump per slot, demand. Demo: 88.9 L/person for every zone on a normal day, 44.4 L on a 6 ML day.
Reference
timetable.cpp: build_timetable(), water_fill()
Follow-up
"Is it optimal?" No: greedy and non-preemptive. Linear programming could optimise; hydraulics are not modelled.
46. How are tanker loads calculated?
Simple
For each zone below the trigger (70 L/person), loads = ⌈(70 − L/person) × population ÷ 10,000⌉.
Deeper
One order per zone per timetable, never duplicated; status planned → dispatched (zone notified) → delivered. On the 6 ML demo day: 103, 167 and 77 loads.
Reference
network.plan_tankers()
Follow-up
"Why 70?" It's a demo value in policy v1, not an official number; the department sets it.
47. How do sensors authenticate, and what if a sensor fails?
Simple
Each device has its own secret key, sent in X-Device-Key; only its SHA-256 hash is stored. A device silent for 30 minutes raises an "offline" alert and staff enter values by hand.
Deeper
Readings are idempotent (UNIQUE(device_id, measured_at) + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING). A level above capacity is refused. The reservoir row is locked, like a commit, so the two never interleave.
Reference
telemetry.ingest(), field_alerts()
Follow-up
"Connected to real SCADA?" No; a simulator stands in. A vendor gateway (OPC UA/Modbus) would post to the same endpoint.
48. How does two-factor sign-in work?
Simple
After the password, the server asks for a 6-digit code from an authenticator app. The code is computed from a shared secret and the current 30-second time step.
Deeper
HMAC-SHA1 of the time-step counter, dynamic truncation, mod 10⁶ (RFC 6238); ±1 step for clock drift; constant-time comparison; a 5-minute challenge with at most 5 attempts under a row lock.
Reference
mfa.py, auth.complete_mfa()
Follow-up
"Where's the weakness?" Secrets are stored unencrypted in the DB; encrypting them is the next step.
49. What is least privilege in your database?
Simple
The running API logs in as jal_app, which can read and change data but can't change the schema, and can't UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE the audit log.
Deeper
Created and granted at start-up by the owner login with GRANT/REVOKE, built safely with PostgreSQL's format(%I, %L). Plus two triggers on the audit log (row and statement level).
Reference
migrations.ensure_app_role(); test test_least_privilege_db_user_cannot_touch_the_audit_log
Follow-up
"Verified in Docker?" The role and its privileges are tested; the API's own connection as jal_app through real psycopg2 is not yet verified.
50. Which DPDP Act features did you implement?
Simple
A versioned privacy notice with consent, "download my data", requests for correction, erasure and grievances, and a retention job.
Deeper
Erasure anonymises the account (keeps the decision records, which the notice explains); retention deletes expired sessions, old read notifications, readings over 400 days, closed issues over 2 years. Incidents show the CERT-In 6 h and Board 72 h deadlines.
Reference
privacy.py, security.py, Compliance tab
Follow-up
"Is it legally compliant?" We can't claim that: the notice text needs legal review and a named grievance officer.
51. Is your system ready for a real department?
Simple
It's ready for a pilot setup on one server, but not for production on its own.
Deeper
Still needed (department's part): CERT-In-empanelled audit, NIC/MeitY hosting, Parichay SSO, real data, an officially approved policy, a shadow-mode pilot. Also unverified on our side: HTTPS profile, backups, Docker on Windows.
Reference
docs/compliance.md "Not in code"
Follow-up
"How would you prove benefit?" Shadow mode for some weeks, then compare the pilot indicators with the decisions actually taken.
52. Which new OS and DBMS concepts does v2.0 add?
Simple
OS: slot scheduling of a shared pump, proportional share with guarantees, a mutex in our rate limiter, monotonic vs wall clock, a background backup process. DBMS: partial unique indexes, HAVING, a window function, a statement-level trigger, GRANT/REVOKE, backup and restore.
Deeper
Locks grew from 10 to 25 FOR UPDATE statements and from 2 to 4 advisory locks.
Reference
Phases 4 J and 5
Follow-up
"Pick one and explain it in depth." The partial unique index for the one active policy is short and convincing.

Ready-to-speak scripts

30-second introduction

"JalRakshak helps a water department share limited water when demand exceeds supply. We modelled it as CPU scheduling: requests are processes, the pipeline is the CPU. Four schedulers in C++, including our Water-aware rule that never leaves anyone with zero, are compared on the same data. Version 2 adds a zone-wise supply timetable with tankers, an approved water policy with maker-checker, officer overrides with recorded reasons, sensor data, and two-factor sign-in, HTTPS, least-privilege database access, backups and DPDP privacy rights. PostgreSQL stores every decision in a locked transaction, so two operators can never hand out the same water twice."

2-minute explanation

Use Phase 1 B, word for word if needed.

5-minute presentation script (with timings)

  1. 0:00–0:30 Problem. "Water stress affects hundreds of millions in India; cities supply water a few hours a day. When there isn't enough, someone decides who gets it, usually by arrival order, without records."
  2. 0:30–1:15 Idea. "We treated it as an OS scheduling problem." Show the analogy table: request = process, pipeline = CPU, litres ÷ 500 = burst time. "Unlike CPU time, water is consumed, so rules also decide how much."
  3. 1:15–2:15 Algorithms and results. Show the 4 Gantt charts / Compare tab. Key point: FCFS leaves 4 of 8 with nothing; the hospital is late. Priority starves the park. Round Robin is fairest (Jain 0.91) but gives the hospital only 70%. Water-aware serves the hospital fully and nobody gets zero, at the cost of longer waits. "No rule wins everything."
  4. 2:15–2:45 v2.0 for a department. Show the Policy tab (maker-checker), the Supply tab (timetable, map, tankers) and a decision record with an override reason.
  5. 2:45–3:15 Safety (DBMS + OS). Explain the commit transaction with SELECT … FOR UPDATE and the child process with pipes. Show the concurrency demo: 80,000 L with locks vs 160,000 L without. Mention CHECK constraints, partial unique indexes and the protected audit log.
  6. 3:15–4:00 Live demo. Sign in as City Hospital → create a request → sign in as admin → Compare → Apply Water-aware → back to the hospital: notification + litres received.
  7. 4:00–4:30 ML. "Random forest forecast, 5.1% error on synthetic hold-out; leak detector precision 0.88. The forecast feeds the scarcity factor."
  8. 4:30–5:00 Honest limits and future. "Synthetic data, demo policy values, no hydraulics; HTTPS and backups configured but not yet run on our machines. Next: verify the deployment, SJF/EDF, real data, and a shadow-mode pilot with a utility, which also needs its security audit, hosting and SSO."

Module-by-module explanation (one line each)

  • Scheduler: pure C++ computation of plans and metrics with invariant checks.
  • Allocation service: builds input from the DB, simulates, commits atomically with locks, notifies.
  • Auth: hashed passwords, hashed sessions, lockout, approval flow, two-factor step, consent.
  • Policy (v2.0): versioned water policy with maker-checker; feeds priorities, shares and weights.
  • Network (v2.0): sources and zones, timetable draft and publish, tankers, zone map.
  • Telemetry (v2.0): device keys, readings, metered consumption, CSV import, field alerts.
  • Privacy and security (v2.0): notice, export, erasure, retention; incidents, rate limiter, operations status.
  • Report (v2.0): decision records and pilot indicators.
  • Portal (user panel): own requests, cancel, issues, notifications, profile.
  • Admin service: accounts, issues, audit list, summary badges.
  • Audit: write-once history and notifications inside the same transaction.
  • DB layer: connection per request (as jal_app), automatic upgrade, app role, bootstrap.
  • ML: synthetic data → leak detection → model comparison → forecast → DB.
  • Frontend: sign-in gate (with 2FA), two panels, one API module, English/Hindi.
  • Infrastructure (v2.0): nginx with CSP, Caddy for HTTPS, a backup container.
  • Experiments: 600 random scenarios comparing rules.

Technology-stack explanation (say it as a chain)

"The browser runs our React app, served by nginx. It calls our FastAPI backend, which runs on Uvicorn. The backend validates input with Pydantic, talks to PostgreSQL through psycopg2, and runs our C++ scheduler as a child process. A separate Python job using pandas and scikit-learn writes forecasts into the same database. Docker Compose starts the services with one command: database, API, ML job, web server and backup process, and with the HTTPS profile also Caddy in front."

OS concepts explanation

"We explicitly implemented FCFS, non-preemptive Priority, Round Robin and a new Water-aware scheduler on a shared simulation engine, with waiting time, utilisation, Jain fairness and starvation metrics. Starvation is prevented by a guarantee floor, our version of aging, which in v2.0 differs by class according to the approved policy. The zone timetable adds slot scheduling: zones are placed in hourly pump capacity, most important first, after shares are fixed by proportional sharing with minimums. At system level, the backend creates a child process for each run and talks to it through pipes, with exit codes and a timeout. Mutual exclusion is achieved with database row locks (25 places), advisory locks and two Python mutexes, one of them in our rate limiter. Deadlock is prevented by a fixed lock order. Memory management and paging are done by the OS; we didn't implement them."

DBMS concepts explanation

"24 tables, mostly in 3NF, with PK, FK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL and 49 CHECK constraints, and partial unique indexes for rules like 'only one active policy'. The M:N between plans and requests is the allocations table. Every change runs in a transaction: the commit locks the reservoir row with SELECT FOR UPDATE, which gives atomicity and isolation at READ COMMITTED and prevents lost updates. A PL/pgSQL trigger makes the audit log append-only. Indexes, including an expression index on lower(email), speed lookups. All queries are parameterised. Migrations are idempotent and run under an advisory lock. The API runs as a least-privilege role created with GRANT and REVOKE, and the database is dumped daily."

Limitations explanation

"Our data is synthetic, so ML accuracy isn't real-world accuracy. Organisation allocation assumes one pipeline at a fixed flow; the timetable has no hydraulics. Deadlines are soft. The policy values are demo placeholders. HTTPS and backups are configured but not yet run on our machines, there's no connection pool, and v2.0 hasn't been deployed for real users or audited."

Future-scope explanation

"First: verify on our machines and in CI, including the HTTPS profile and a backup restore. Then: connection pooling, shorter locks, SJF and EDF, timetable rotation. Then: per-request explanations, notifications by SMS/email, encrypted 2FA secrets. Finally, with a water utility: real data, an approved policy, audit, government hosting and SSO, and a shadow-mode pilot."

Difficult questions to rehearse

  1. "Paging kahan hai?" → it isn't in our code; explain the distinction.
  2. "Your RR wait time: is it really waiting time?" → it's response time.
  3. "Why is Water-aware's average wait the worst?" → it serves important users fully and reserves floors, so others wait. That's the trade-off.
  4. "Show me a race condition in your code without locks." → the concurrency demo.
  5. "Is allocations in 3NF?" → no: reservoir_id is a deliberate exception.
  6. "What if the scheduler hangs?" → 10 s timeout, kill, rollback, 500.
  7. "Why do you trust the frontend?" → we don't; roles are checked on the server.
  8. "Is 0.3 optimal?" → no single optimum; it's a policy trade-off (floor table).
  9. "What's novel?" → be modest; the floor plus measured trade-off.
  10. "Did you test on Windows?" → answer truthfully.
  11. "Can the same officer propose and approve?" → no, 403; show it.
  12. "Your timetable gives North the morning every day: is that fair?" → it's greedy by priority then zone id; rotation is future work.
  13. "Is HTTPS working?" → configured with Caddy, not yet run on our machines.

Phase 10 wrap-up

Summary. 52 graded questions with answers (12 on v2.0); 30-second, 2-minute and 5-minute scripts; one-paragraph explanations for modules, stack, OS, DBMS, limits and future. Honesty is your strongest viva tool.

Remember:

  • say the simple answer first;
  • always name the file or function;
  • admit what isn't verified;
  • the numbers to quote: 80k vs 160k L; 0 unserved; MAE 1,223 L (5.1%); 88.9 L/person per zone on a normal demo day; 77 backend tests.
1. In one sentence, which OS concepts did you implement yourself?The scheduling policies (FCFS, non-preemptive Priority, Round Robin, Water-aware) with their metrics and starvation prevention, as a simulation of water delivery.
2. Best evidence of concurrency safety?The 4-thread commit test, plus the demo: with locks 1 plan and 80,000 L; without locks 2 plans and 160,000 L.
3. Weakest part, in one line?Synthetic data and demo policy values. Technically: no pool, HTTPS and backups not yet run, Allocate tab on reservoir 1 only.
4. What's the honest novelty claim?A simple, tunable guarantee floor for a consumable resource, plus a measured importance-vs-fairness trade-off. It's an engineering combination of known ideas, not a proven new algorithm.
5. What would you demo live in 45 seconds?Hospital creates a request → admin compares and applies Water-aware → hospital sees the notification and litres received (and the audit log entry). For v2.0: compute and publish a timetable with a low release, plan tankers, and show the hospital's supply hours on its Home page.

Phase 11 · Concept learning mode

Each difficult concept is taught in 10 steps:

  1. simple definition
  2. everyday analogy
  3. technical explanation
  4. example from JalRakshak
  5. code or SQL
  6. step-by-step execution
  7. common mistakes
  8. difference from similar concepts
  9. a practical question
  10. a viva question with its answer

Read slowly; try step 9 yourself before the answer.

Concept 1: Process, child process and pipes

1 Definition
A process is a running program. A child process is one started by another process (its parent). A pipe is a one-way channel: what one process writes, the other reads.
2 Analogy
You (parent) call a plumber (child). You pass the problem through a letterbox (stdin pipe); the plumber passes the bill back through another slot (stdout pipe) and gives a thumbs-up or thumbs-down (exit code).
3 Technical
The kernel gives each process its own memory and file-descriptor table. A pipe is a kernel buffer with a read end and a write end. When the parent creates the child, it connects the pipe ends to the child's fd 0 (stdin) and fd 1 (stdout). The parent later waits to collect the exit status.
4 In JalRakshak
Every simulate or commit starts jalrakshak-scheduler as a child of the Python backend.
5 Code
proc = subprocess.run([binary], input=json.dumps(payload), capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
6 Steps
  1. Python creates pipes.
  2. The kernel starts the child running the binary.
  3. Python writes JSON and closes stdin.
  4. The child reads until end of input, computes, writes JSON, and returns 0.
  5. Python reads stdout, collects the exit status, and parses the result.
7 Mistakes
Saying "we implemented fork()" (we didn't; the library did). Forgetting the timeout (a stuck child would hang the request while locks are held). Using shell=True (injection risk).
8 Vs similar
Thread: shares memory, same process. Process: separate memory. Pipe vs socket: a pipe connects related processes on one machine; a socket can connect any processes, even across a network (we use sockets for HTTP and the DB).
9 Practice
What exit code does the scheduler return for unknown command-line flags, and why does it differ from an input error? (Answer: 2 for usage errors, 1 for input/processing errors with error JSON. This lets the caller tell "called wrongly" apart from "bad data".)
10 Viva
Q: Why is a separate process safer than calling C++ code inside Python? A: If the C++ crashes or loops, only the child is affected. The parent kills it after 10 s and rolls back, and the API stays up.

Concept 2: Starvation and aging (our guarantee floor)

1 Definition
Starvation: a job waits forever (or, for water, gets nothing). Aging: gradually increasing the priority of waiting jobs so they eventually run.
2 Analogy
At a wedding buffet the VIPs go first; if VIPs keep arriving, regular guests never eat. Rule: "everyone gets at least one plate reserved".
3 Technical
Static-priority schedulers starve low-priority work when high-priority work keeps coming. Fixes: aging (priority grows with waiting time), fair-share scheduling, reservations. For a consumable resource, a reservation is needed: the water must be held back before it's used up.
4 In JalRakshak
Priority leaves 3 of 8 with nothing; Water-aware leaves 0. Deadline pressure grows as time passes (aging-like), and the floor reserves 30% for everyone still waiting.
5 Code
cap = max(floor × asked, water_left − floor × others_still_asking) in water_aware.cpp
6 Steps (sample)
  • After the hospital, Shanti and Rajpur are served, 13,000 L is left.
  • The others ask 37,000 L in total; 30% of that = 11,100 L is reserved.
  • The school can take at most 13,000 − 11,100 = 1,900 L.
  • Each later request gets about its 30%.
  • Final: no zeros.
7 Mistakes
Saying "Round Robin has no starvation, so it's best". It also ignores importance (the hospital gets only 70%). Also, a floor too high (0.5) makes everything equal and ignores priority.
8 Vs similar
Starvation (someone waits forever while others progress) vs deadlock (nobody progresses) vs livelock (everyone is busy but nothing gets done).
9 Practice
If the floor were 0, what would Water-aware become? (Pure score order: the most unequal, closest to Priority. Experiments: 4.29 requests left with nothing under severe scarcity.)
10 Viva
Q: Is the floor the same as aging? A: Same purpose (prevent starvation), different mechanism: aging changes the order over time; the floor reserves a minimum amount, which a consumable resource needs.

Concept 3: Race condition and critical section

1 Definition
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on timing between concurrent operations. A critical section is the code that must run by one at a time to avoid it.
2 Analogy
Two people book the last train seat at the same second on two counters. Both see "1 seat free"; both get a ticket.
3 Technical
The classic pattern is read → decide → write. If two actors interleave between read and write, one decision is based on stale data. Fix: mutual exclusion (locks) around read-decide-write, or atomic operations.
4 In JalRakshak
Two admins applying plans. Also: login failure counters, the "max 5 pending" check, the schema upgrade.
5 Code
SELECT reservoir_id, available_litres FROM reservoirs WHERE reservoir_id = %s FOR UPDATE
6 Steps
Without the lock:
  • T1 reads 8 pending; T2 reads 8 pending.
  • Both plan; both write → double allocation (demo: 160,000 L).
With the lock:
  • T2 waits at the SELECT until T1 commits.
  • Then T2 reads 0 pending → 409.
7 Mistakes
Thinking a CHECK constraint is enough (it only stops negative water). Locking in Python only (doesn't work across processes or machines). Holding locks during slow work unnecessarily.
8 Vs similar
Race condition (the bug) vs critical section (the protected region) vs mutex (the tool) vs atomicity (all-or-nothing, a different guarantee: a transaction can be atomic and still race without locks).
9 Practice
Why does auth.login() lock the account row? (Two parallel wrong guesses could both read 4 failures and both write 5, so the lockout could be skipped or miscounted.)
10 Viva
Q: Where does your critical section start and end? A: From the FOR UPDATE on the reservoir row to COMMIT/ROLLBACK at the end of the with conn: block in commit_allocation().

Concept 4: Deadlock

1 Definition
Two or more processes each wait for something another holds, so none can continue.
2 Analogy
Two people in a corridor, each politely waiting for the other to move first, forever.
3 Technical
It needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Strategies: prevention (break a condition), avoidance (Banker's algorithm), detection + recovery (wait-for graph, abort a victim).
4 In JalRakshak
Prevention: a fixed lock order (reservoir → requests). Detection: PostgreSQL's built-in deadlock detector (error 40P01).
5 Code
In commit_allocation(): first … reservoirs … FOR UPDATE, then _fetch_pending(cur, rid, lock=True) (FOR UPDATE OF r, ordered by arrival and id).
6 Steps
  • T1 locks the reservoir.
  • T2 requests the reservoir and waits (it holds nothing yet, so there's no cycle).
  • T1 locks the requests, writes, commits.
  • T2 proceeds.
7 Mistakes
Claiming "deadlocks are impossible". Rather: "we prevent the common cycle, and the DBMS detects any other".
8 Vs similar
Deadlock (stuck forever) vs blocking (normal waiting that ends when the other finishes).
9 Practice
Which Coffman condition would you break by having transactions request all locks at once? (Hold and wait.)
10 Viva
Q: What happens to the user if PostgreSQL aborts their transaction because of a deadlock? A: Rollback, nothing saved; HTTP 500 with the database error; they can retry. Automatic retry is a possible improvement.

Concept 5: Transactions and ACID

1 Definition
A transaction is a group of database operations treated as one unit: either all happen or none do.
2 Analogy
A bank transfer: debit A and credit B. Debit without credit is unacceptable.
3 Technical
  • Atomicity: undo on failure.
  • Consistency: constraints hold.
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work.
  • Durability: once committed, the change survives crashes (the WAL is written to disk first).
4 In JalRakshak
Applying a plan writes 6 kinds of rows. All of them or none.
5 Code
with conn: + with conn.cursor() as cur:. psycopg2 begins on the first statement, commits at the end of the block, and rolls back on an exception.
6 Steps
BEGIN → lock → plan → INSERT run → INSERT allocations → UPDATE requests → UPDATE reservoir → INSERT notifications → INSERT audit → COMMIT. Any failure → ROLLBACK.
7 Mistakes
Thinking "atomic" means "isolated". Committing after each statement (autocommit) inside a multi-step change.
8 Vs similar
Transaction (unit of work) vs lock (concurrency tool used inside transactions) vs constraint (a rule checked at statement time).
9 Practice
If inserting notifications fails after the reservoir was updated, what is in the DB? (Nothing from this attempt: everything is rolled back, and the water level is unchanged.)
10 Viva
Q: Which ACID property does PostgreSQL give you without any code? A: Durability (WAL), and atomicity once we define the transaction boundary. Isolation needs our locks for correctness in this case.

Concept 6: Isolation levels and READ COMMITTED

1 Definition
An isolation level decides how much one transaction can see of others' changes.
2 Analogy
Exam hall rules: can you see a classmate's answer only after they submit (committed), or even while they're writing (uncommitted)?
3 Technical
The SQL standard defines four levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads). In READ COMMITTED, each statement sees data committed before it started. A statement waiting on a row lock re-checks the newest version of that row.
4 In JalRakshak
The default level is used. Correctness comes from FOR UPDATE locks plus that re-check.
5 Code
SHOW default_transaction_isolation; → read committed (checked on the test server).
6 Steps
  • T2 waits on a request row locked by T1.
  • T1 commits status = 'approved'.
  • T2 re-evaluates WHERE status = 'pending' on the new version, which no longer matches.
  • The row is skipped, so T2 sees 0 pending.
7 Mistakes
Believing READ COMMITTED alone prevents lost updates (it doesn't without locks). Believing SERIALIZABLE is "free" (it causes aborts that need retries).
8 Vs similar
Isolation level (visibility policy) vs lock (explicit mutual exclusion) vs MVCC (the versioning mechanism behind visibility).
9 Practice
Which anomaly is allowed in our commit and harmless? (Phantom: a new request inserted during a commit isn't planned and stays pending.)
10 Viva
Q: Why not SERIALIZABLE? A: Row locks already serialise the conflicting part. SERIALIZABLE would add abort-and-retry handling with no extra safety for this workload.

Concept 7: Functional dependency and normalisation

1 Definition
A functional dependency X → Y means X's value determines Y's value. Normalisation organises tables so each fact is stored once.
2 Analogy
Your roll number determines your name. If your name is written in 20 registers and you change it, you must update all 20 (an update anomaly).
3 Technical
  • 1NF: atomic values.
  • 2NF: no partial dependency on a composite key.
  • 3NF: no transitive dependency (non-key → non-key).
  • BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key.
4 In JalRakshak
zone_id → population is stored only in zones; requests reach it by join.
5 Code
JOIN zones z ON z.zone_id = u.zone_id in PENDING_SQL instead of copying the population into each request.
6 Steps
List the FDs → find the keys → check each non-key column depends on "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key".
7 Mistakes
Calling every redundancy a bug. Our allocations.reservoir_id and audit_log.actor are deliberate denormalisations with reasons.
8 Vs similar
Normalisation (remove redundancy) vs denormalisation (add controlled redundancy for speed or history).
9 Practice
If we stored zone_population in water_requests, which anomaly appears? (An update anomaly: changing the zone population would require updating every request, and old requests could disagree.)
10 Viva
Q: Is users in 3NF given user_type and priority? A: Yes. user_type doesn't determine priority (the admin can change it per organisation), so there's no transitive FD.

Concept 8: Index (B-tree)

1 Definition
A separate sorted structure that lets the DBMS find rows without scanning the whole table.
2 Analogy
The index at the back of a textbook: look up "deadlock" → page 214, instead of reading every page.
3 Technical
A balanced tree of pages; leaves hold sorted keys and row pointers (TIDs); lookup O(log n). It must be updated on every insert or update (write cost). The planner decides whether using it is cheaper than a sequential scan.
4 In JalRakshak
idx_requests_status finds pending requests; accounts_email_key on lower(email) enables case-insensitive login and uniqueness.
5 Code
CREATE INDEX idx_requests_status ON water_requests(status);
6 Steps (real EXPLAIN)
Bitmap Index Scan on idx_requests_status → Bitmap Heap Scan on water_requests → joins via users_pkey, zones_pkey → Sort.
7 Mistakes
Indexing every column (slows writes). Expecting an index on a 10-row table to be used (a sequential scan is cheaper there).
8 Vs similar
Index vs key: a key is a logical rule (uniqueness, reference); an index is a physical structure (PostgreSQL creates one automatically for each PK and UNIQUE).
9 Practice
Why lower(email) rather than email? (So lookup and uniqueness ignore case: "A@x.com" equals "a@x.com".)
10 Viva
Q: Clustered index in PostgreSQL? A: PostgreSQL tables are heaps. All indexes are secondary; CLUSTER reorders a table once but doesn't maintain it.

Concept 9: Password hashing and session tokens

1 Definition
Hashing turns a password into a fixed fingerprint that can't be reversed. A session token is a random secret proving you signed in.
2 Analogy
The bank keeps a fingerprint of your signature, not your pen. After you show ID once, you get a visitor badge (token) for the day.
3 Technical
  • PBKDF2-SHA256 repeats hashing 600,000 times with a random salt, so guessing is slow and identical passwords give different hashes.
  • Comparison is constant-time (hmac.compare_digest), so the comparison time reveals nothing about the hash.
  • The token is 32 random bytes; only SHA-256(token) is stored.
4 In JalRakshak
auth.hash_password, verify_password, _create_session, account_for_token.
5 Code
Stored format: pbkdf2_sha256$600000$<salt>$<hash>
6 Steps
  1. Login: read the salt and iterations from the stored string.
  2. Recompute the hash and compare.
  3. Create a token; store its SHA-256; return the token once.
  4. Each later request: hash the presented token, look it up, check expiry and that the account is active.
7 Mistakes
Encrypting passwords (reversible) instead of hashing. Storing raw tokens. Using random instead of secrets.
8 Vs similar
Hashing (one-way) vs encryption (two-way with a key) vs encoding (base64; no secrecy at all).
9 Practice
Why is a slow hash good here but bad for the token lookup? (Passwords have low entropy and need slowing down against guessing. Tokens are 256-bit random values that can't be guessed, so a fast SHA-256 is fine.)
10 Viva
Q: If someone steals the DB, can they sign in? A: Not directly: they get password hashes (slow to crack) and token hashes (useless as tokens).

Concept 10: Jain fairness index

1 Definition
A number from 1/n to 1 showing how equal the shares are; 1 = everyone got the same fraction of what they asked.
2 Analogy
Cutting a cake: 1.0 if every plate gets the same share of what each person wanted; low if a few plates get everything.
3 Technical
J = (Σxᵢ)² / (n·Σxᵢ²), where xᵢ = got/asked for request i.
4 In JalRakshak
FCFS 0.50, Priority 0.57, Water-aware 0.74, Round Robin 0.91 on the sample.
5 Code
m.jain_fairness = (sum_x * sum_x) / (n * sum_x2) in compute_metrics().
6 Steps (FCFS)
  • x = [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0].
  • Σx = 4, Σx² = 4.
  • J = 16 / (8 × 4) = 0.50.
7 Mistakes
Treating fairness as the only goal. Equal shares can still be bad if the hospital needed 100%.
8 Vs similar
Jain (equality) vs importance-weighted satisfaction (equality weighted by priority) vs utilisation (how much water was used at all).
9 Practice
What is J if every request gets exactly 62.5%? (1.0: perfectly equal.)
10 Viva
Q: Why isn't Round Robin your recommended rule if it's the fairest? A: It ignores importance and deadlines. Our goal balances fairness with protecting essential users.

Concept 11: Maker-checker (separation of duties) v2.0

1 Definition
An important change needs two different people: one makes (proposes) it, another checks (approves) it.
2 Analogy
A bank cheque above a limit needs two signatures. One clerk can't both write and authorise it.
3 Technical
A state machine (draft → pending → approved / rejected; approved → superseded) plus an identity check at the approve step, inside one transaction, with every step audited.
4 In JalRakshak
Water policy changes: the policy decides every organisation's priority and guaranteed share, so one officer alone must not change it.
5 Code
if p["proposed_by"] == actor["account_id"] and config.REQUIRE_SECOND_APPROVER: raise Forbidden("maker-checker: …") in policy.decide().
6 Steps
admin creates a draft → submits (pending) → tries to approve: 403 → approver approves: old policy superseded, new one approved, class priorities copied to organisations, audit rows and notifications.
7 Mistakes
Checking the role only ("is an admin") instead of the person; checking it in the frontend only; forgetting that two approvals can run at once (we lock the active policy and have a partial unique index).
8 Vs similar
Maker-checker (two people, one decision) vs RBAC (which role may do what) vs 2FA (proving one person's identity twice).
9 Practice
With REQUIRE_SECOND_APPROVER=0, what does the audit log show when an admin approves their own proposal? (policy.approve with "self_approved": true.)
10 Viva
Q: Why not maker-checker on every plan commit? A: Plans are daily operations and must be fast; the policy that drives them is approved by two people, and overrides need a recorded reason. A threshold-based second approval for large overrides is a sensible extension.

Concept 12: Partial unique index v2.0

1 Definition
A unique index that covers only the rows matching a WHERE condition, so uniqueness is enforced only among those rows.
2 Analogy
A school can have many former head-teachers but only one current head-teacher. Uniqueness applies only to "current".
3 Technical
PostgreSQL stores only matching rows in the index; an INSERT/UPDATE that would create a duplicate key among them fails with 23505. Indexing a constant ((TRUE)) means "at most one such row at all".
4 In JalRakshak
Exactly one approved policy; at most one published timetable per date.
5 SQL
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX policies_one_active ON policies ((TRUE)) WHERE status = 'approved';
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX timetables_one_published ON supply_timetables (for_date) WHERE status = 'published';
6 Steps
approve v2 → in the same transaction v1 becomes superseded (leaves the index) and v2 becomes approved (enters it) → COMMIT: one row in the index. Any path that tried to approve without superseding would fail.
7 Mistakes
A normal UNIQUE (status) would allow only one superseded and one rejected policy ever; doing the order wrong in one statement (approve before supersede) would trip the index.
8 Vs similar
vs a CHECK constraint (looks at one row only, can't compare rows) vs a trigger (can, but more code and race-prone) vs a normal UNIQUE (all rows).
9 Practice
Write an index that allows many draft timetables but only one published per date. (The second one above.)
10 Viva
Q: Why not just check in Python? A: Python checks can race between two transactions; the database index can't be bypassed by any code path.

Concept 13: Weighted water-filling and slot scheduling v2.0

1 Definition
Water-filling shares a budget among consumers in proportion to weights, but never gives anyone more than they need; surplus from capped consumers is re-shared. Slot scheduling then books each consumer's amount into time slots of a shared resource.
2 Analogy
Pouring juice into glasses of different sizes, more for the bigger thirsts; when a small glass is full you keep pouring into the others. Then booking the single tap for each glass.
3 Technical
Loop: each active zone would get pool × wᵢ/Σw; if that exceeds its room, give it exactly its room and mark it inactive, then recompute; when nobody is capped, split the pool and stop. Then place zones (priority order) into the earliest run of hourly slots with enough free pump capacity.
4 In JalRakshak
The daily zone timetable: floors first (30% of each zone's target in policy v1), then water-filling with weight = priority × (1 − floor) × target.
5 Code
water_fill() and step 2 of build_timetable() in timetable.cpp.
6 Steps (toy)
  • Budget 10 L, three zones with room 6, 6 and 2, equal weights.
  • Equal split would be 3.33 each, but zone 3 only needs 2 → give 2, it's full.
  • 8 L left for zones 1 and 2 → 4 each (under their room of 6) → result [4, 4, 2].
7 Mistakes
Splitting proportionally once and ignoring caps (zone 3 would get 3.33 L it can't use, wasting water); placing zones without checking pump capacity per slot.
8 Vs similar
vs Round Robin (equal turns, no weights) vs Priority (all to the most important first) vs max-min fairness (water-filling with equal weights).
9 Practice
Budget 9, rooms [6, 6, 6], weights [2, 1, 0]? (Zone 3 has weight 0 and gets nothing; zones 1 and 2 split 9 as 6 and 3; zone 1 is exactly full.)
10 Viva
Q: Which OS idea is closest? A: Proportional-share scheduling with reservations (weights plus guaranteed minimums, as in Linux CFS weights and cgroup minimums), followed by non-preemptive slot booking.

Concept 14: Time-based one-time passwords (TOTP) v2.0

1 Definition
A 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds, computed from a secret shared once between the server and the user's phone.
2 Analogy
Two people with identical code books who both turn to the page for "this half-minute"; neither needs to call the other.
3 Technical
counter = ⌊unix time ÷ 30⌋; h = HMAC-SHA1(secret, counter as 8 bytes); take 4 bytes at offset (last byte & 15), clear the top bit, mod 10⁶ (RFC 4226 + RFC 6238).
4 In JalRakshak
Two-factor sign-in for administrators (and anyone who turns it on).
5 Code
mfa.code_at(), mfa.verify() (accepts counter −1, 0, +1, compares with hmac.compare_digest).
6 Steps (RFC test vector)
With the RFC's test secret (Base32 GEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQGEZDGNBVGY3TQOJQ) at time 59 s, counter = 1 and our code_at() returns 287082, the last 6 digits of the RFC's published value 94287082. At time 1,111,111,109 it returns 081804 (RFC: 07081804). Checked on 18 Oct 2026.
7 Mistakes
Comparing with == (timing leak); no drift window (codes fail when clocks differ by seconds); allowing unlimited attempts; issuing the session before the code is checked.
8 Vs similar
TOTP (time counter) vs HOTP (event counter) vs SMS OTP (server sends a code; needs a gateway, can be intercepted) vs password (static).
9 Practice
Why does the server accept 3 codes at any moment? (Previous, current and next 30-second step, for clock drift.)
10 Viva
Q: Can an attacker who steals one code reuse it? A: Only within its ~90-second window, and only with the password and a fresh challenge; blocking reuse of the same code is a listed improvement.

Concept 15: Least privilege with GRANT and REVOKE v2.0

1 Definition
Every component gets only the permissions it needs, nothing more.
2 Analogy
A cashier can open the till but not the vault, and can't erase the CCTV recording.
3 Technical
PostgreSQL roles own objects; other roles get privileges with GRANT and lose them with REVOKE. Only the owner (or a superuser) can ALTER or DROP a table. Triggers still apply to every role.
4 In JalRakshak
The API runs as jal_app: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on data tables; on audit_log only SELECT and INSERT; no TRUNCATE; no schema changes. Upgrades use the owner login.
5 SQL
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO jal_app; REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE ON audit_log FROM jal_app;
6 Steps
start-up with owner → migrate → ensure_app_role() creates or updates the role and grants → normal requests connect as jal_app → a bug or injected statement like DELETE FROM audit_log fails with "permission denied" (and the trigger would refuse it anyway).
7 Mistakes
Running the app as postgres (v1.0 did); building GRANT statements by pasting names into strings (we use format(%I, %L)); forgetting to grant on tables added later (we re-grant on every start).
8 Vs similar
DB privileges (what SQL a login may run) vs application roles (what an API user may do) vs row-level security (which rows a login may see).
9 Practice
Which of these can jal_app do: insert an audit row, delete a notification, create a table? (Yes, yes, no.)
10 Viva
Q: If you already check roles in Python, why bother? A: Defence in depth: if the application is compromised or has a bug, the database still limits the damage.

Concept 16: Sliding-window rate limiting (and why it needs a mutex) v2.0

1 Definition
Allow at most N requests per client in any 60-second window; refuse the rest with HTTP 429.
2 Analogy
A ticket counter that serves each person at most 20 times an hour; the guard keeps a list of times you came.
3 Technical
Per (address, bucket) a deque of timestamps: drop those older than 60 s from the left, refuse if the length is already N, else append now. Using time.monotonic() so clock changes can't reset it.
4 In JalRakshak
Sign-in endpoints 20/min, the rest of the API 600/min, per client address (from X-Forwarded-For only behind the trusted proxy).
5 Code
security.RateLimiter.allow(); middleware security_headers in main.py.
6 Steps
request → bucket by path → lock → clean old hits → count → 429 or record and continue → headers added to the response.
7 Mistakes
No lock (two threads both see 19 and both pass: a race condition); a fixed window (bursts at the boundary); trusting X-Forwarded-For from anyone; keeping counters only in one process when several run.
8 Vs similar
Rate limit (per client, per time) vs account lockout (per account, after failures) vs semaphore (limits concurrent users, not requests per minute).
9 Practice
Limit 3: hits at t = 100, 101, 102; is t = 103 allowed? t = 161? (No; yes, because the hit at 100 has left the window. This is exactly the unit test.)
10 Viva
Q: Where is the critical section? A: Inside with self._lock: in allow(): reading, trimming, counting and appending to the shared deque must happen as one step.

Phase 11 wrap-up

Summary. Sixteen core concepts (6 new in v2.0), each tied to a specific line of your code and a real number from your tests.

Remember: for every concept, be able to give the analogy, the file, and the "vs similar" difference. That is what examiners probe.

1. Child process vs thread in one line?A child process has its own memory and talks via pipes; a thread shares memory with others in the same process.
2. Compute J for x = [1, 0.5].Σx = 1.5, Σx² = 1.25, n = 2 → 2.25 / 2.5 = 0.9.
3. Which index makes sign-in case-insensitive?The UNIQUE expression index accounts_email_key ON accounts (lower(email)).
4. What makes PBKDF2 slow, and why is that good?600,000 iterations; it slows offline guessing if the hashes leak.
4b. Water-fill a budget of 12 into rooms [10, 2, 2] with equal weights.Equal split 4 each; zones 2 and 3 need only 2 → give 2 each; 8 left for zone 1 (room 10) → [8, 2, 2].
4c. Partial unique index vs CHECK constraint?A CHECK looks at one row; a partial unique index enforces uniqueness among the rows that match its WHERE, so it can say "only one approved policy".
5. Starvation vs deadlock?Starvation: some never get served while others progress. Deadlock: a set of processes can't progress at all because they wait on each other.

Phase 12 · Final project knowledge document

A compact reference, consistent with the source code (v2.0, commit 9b05e7a) and the earlier phases. Use it for revision; the phases above have the details.

1. Abstract

JalRakshak is a web-based decision-support system for sharing scarce water in a city. At the organisation level it models each water request as a process and the supply pipeline as a CPU, and implements four scheduling policies in C++17 on a shared discrete-event engine:

  • First Come First Served;
  • non-preemptive Priority;
  • Round Robin (2,000 L quantum);
  • a new Water-aware policy, which combines five weighted factors with a guaranteed share per class of organisation that prevents starvation.

Version 2.0 adds a zone level: a daily supply timetable that shares each source's release among zones (guaranteed shares plus weighted water-filling) and places them in hourly blocks within pump and inlet capacity, with tanker orders for zones below a per-person trigger. Priorities, shares, norm and weights come from a versioned water policy approved by two officers (maker-checker). Officers may override a plan with a recorded reason; each applied plan stores its policy, the override and the metrics of all alternatives, and can be printed as a decision record.

A FastAPI backend runs the scheduler as a child process connected by pipes and stores each decision in PostgreSQL inside a single transaction with row-level locks, so concurrent operators can't allocate the same water twice. Sensors and meters push readings with per-device keys. Security and privacy include TOTP two-factor sign-in, rate limiting, a strict Content-Security-Policy, an HTTPS proxy, a least-privilege database role, daily backups, DPDP consent/export/erasure, retention and an incident register. A Python ML pipeline forecasts demand (random forest, MAE 1,223 L / 5.1% on synthetic data) and detects possible leaks (precision 0.88, recall 0.66), using real meter data where a zone has 120 days of it.

Across 600 synthetic scenarios, Water-aware left no request without water under moderate or severe scarcity. Round Robin was fairest; Priority delivered most to important users under severe scarcity. All results are on generated data; no field deployment has been made.

2. Problem statement

When available water is less than demand, utilities must decide who receives how much and when, both among organisations and among zones of the city, and must be able to justify those decisions. Simple rules ignore importance or starve less important users; decisions are rarely compared, approved, recorded, or protected against concurrent errors. Context: about 600 million Indians face high to extreme water stress (NITI Aayog CWMI 2018, as reported), and cities such as Delhi and Bengaluru supply water a few hours a day on average (2023 study).

3. Objectives

  1. Implement FCFS, Priority, Round Robin and a new Water-aware rule on one engine, and measure them (wait, utilisation, satisfaction, importance-weighted delivery, Jain fairness, starvation, deadline misses).
  2. Guarantee no double allocation under concurrency.
  3. Forecast demand and flag leaks.
  4. Provide secure user and admin panels with auditing.
  5. (v2.0) Make decisions policy-driven and accountable: maker-checker policy, overrides with reasons, decision records, pilot indicators.
  6. (v2.0) Plan zone-wise supply hours within source, pump and inlet limits, with tankers.
  7. (v2.0) Accept field data, and meet government expectations for security and privacy.

4. Scope

In: organisation-level allocation (reservoir 1 in the UI); multi-source zone timetables and tankers; policy and approvals; decision records; sensors, meters, CSV import, zone map; ML on generated or real data; two panels (English/Hindi user panel); security and privacy features; local Docker deployment with optional HTTPS and backups.

Out: controlling pumps and valves; pipe hydraulics; billing; real SCADA connection; production hosting, audit and SSO (the department's part).

5. Functional modules

  • Scheduler (C++): 4 rules, manual mode, timetable
  • Allocation service (simulate, commit with overrides, shadow)
  • Policy (maker-checker)
  • Network: sources, zones, timetable, tankers, map
  • Telemetry: devices, readings, metered consumption, CSV import, field alerts
  • Authentication and accounts (with 2FA and consent)
  • User portal; admin services (accounts, issues, audit)
  • Privacy (notice, export, requests, retention); security (incidents, rate limit, operations)
  • Reports (decision records, pilot indicators)
  • ML pipeline; experiments
  • Frontend (two panels, 11 admin tabs, i18n)
  • Database and migrations; infrastructure (nginx CSP, Caddy, backup)

6. Technology stack

  • C++17 (g++, Make, own JSON parser)
  • Python 3.12; FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic; psycopg2; standard-library crypto (hmac, hashlib, secrets)
  • PostgreSQL 16 (SQL, PL/pgSQL, DCL)
  • pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib
  • React 19 + esbuild
  • nginx (CSP template); Caddy (HTTPS, optional); pg_dump backup container
  • Docker + Compose; GitHub Actions (configured, not yet run); PowerShell scripts

7. Architecture

Three tiers (React → FastAPI → PostgreSQL) plus a C++ child-process scheduler, a one-shot ML job and a backup process, in Docker services; Caddy in front in the HTTPS profile.

  • Browser ↔ API: JSON over HTTP(S) with Bearer tokens.
  • Gateway → API: readings with X-Device-Key.
  • API ↔ scheduler: pipes + exit code + 10 s timeout; modes plan and timetable.
  • API ↔ DB: as jal_app; owner login only for upgrades.
  • ML and API communicate only through the database.
